title: Drone-PUR: From Visual Clue Discovery to Understanding and Reasoning in UAV Scenes
summary: The reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) can be limited by incomplete or inaccurate visual observations in the general domain. In unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) scenes, small targets, subtle attributes, and changing viewpoints further complicate perception and understanding. Therefore, we introduce Drone-PUR, a dataset and benchmark organized around visual clue discovery, interpretation, and integration, corresponding to the three capability dimensions of perception, understanding, and reasoning. Reasoning samples are designed to require models to combine multiple visual clues to derive visually grounded conclusions. Its 11 tasks provide 175k training and 20k test samples spanning single images, image sequences, cross-modal images, and multiple viewpoints. All test samples undergo human review. Evaluating 22 general-purpose VLMs reveals persistent limitations in spatial judgment and cross-modal and cross-view reasoning. Across models, stronger perception is associated with better reasoning, while single-task fine-tuning further reveals selective bidirectional transfer between these capabilities. To examine domain adaptation, we develop UAV-PUR from Qwen3-VL through staged fine-tuning with auxiliary supervision. Its 4B and 8B variants improve overall multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points over their pretrained counterparts, respectively. The dataset and project resources are available at https://drone-pur.github.io.

Introduction ecent advances in multimodal learning have enabled vision--language models (VLMs) to combine visual perception with language understanding, supporting complex reasoning and task execution. These capabilities enable unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) applications, including navigation~ TravelUAV , anomaly understanding~ A2Seek , and object search~ ji2026towards . However, VLMs' strong reasoning capabilities do not guarantee reliable inference from images. Previous studies~ eagle,VisuRiddles,MathVerse on general-domain visual reasoning have shown that fine-grained perception errors can undermine subsequent inference. Compared with general-domain imagery, UAV images often contain small, densely distributed targets that occupy few pixels, yet their subtle attributes may be critical for identifying objects and interpreting their states and behaviors. Changes in UAV viewpoints can also alter object appearance and spatial reference frames, leading to spatial disorientation. These characteristics can obscure key visual clues and hinder their semantic and spatial alignment, leaving subsequent reasoning grounded in incomplete or incorrect visual information. Cross-view, cross-modal, or cross-frame inputs further require models to associate complementary clues across observations. Evaluating reasoning in UAV scenes therefore requires examining the visual capabilities that underpin it, including how models discover and interpret visual clues and integrate observations to support their inferences. Recent UAV benchmarks have expanded evaluation from perception to spatial understanding, collaborative understanding, and task planning. UAVBench~ UAVIT-1M and UAVQA-Bench~ UAVQA-Bench assess image-level and region-level understanding, while MM-UAVBench~ Mm-uavbench extends capability evaluation to cognition and planning. Other studies investigate spatial and spatiotemporal understanding~ SpatialSky,SpatialUAV,open3d,urbanvideo , as well as embodied tasks~ CityEQA,Embodiedcity . Collaborative understanding is further investigated through multi-drone observations and cross-platform image pairs~ Aircopbench,LinkS2,Urbench . Despite this expanding scope of evaluation, further systematic study is needed to clarify how VLMs differ in discovering, interpreting, and integrating UAV visual clues, how these abilities relate, and whether domain-specific training can improve them jointly and enable cross-task transfer. To investigate these questions, we introduce Drone-PUR, a UAV dataset and benchmark organized across three capability dimensions: Perception, Understanding, and Reasoning. These dimensions are distinguished by the roles that visual clues play in forming an answer. In this work, we define a visual clue as a task-relevant image region containing an individual object or a group of objects and associated with a specific modality, viewpoint, and capture time. Perception discovers and recognizes visual clues and extracts basic information, including categories, attributes, counts, and locations. Understanding aligns these clues with the semantic conditions and spatial concepts. Reasoning connects multiple visual clues through logical inference to form visually grounded explanations or conclusions. Fig.~ fig_1 (a) illustrates these dimensions within the same UAV scene: models identify ducks and fences, interpret the enclosure structure, spatial layout, and signs of human activity, and combine these observations to explain why all the ducks are concentrated in the pond. This organization allows us to examine both dimension-specific challenges and interactions among capabilities. Drone-PUR instantiates the three capability dimensions through 11 tasks spanning single images, image sequences, paired RGB and thermal infrared (TIR) observations, and synchronized UAV views. It integrates images from eight UAV datasets we previously released with 66,940 newly collected images, yielding 175k training samples and 20k test samples across diverse scenes. Over 90 of the annotated task-relevant regions occupy less than 1 of the image area, highlighting the fine-grained visual demands of Drone-PUR. The four reasoning tasks in Drone-PUR cover causal explanations and situational inference within single images, as well as clue integration across modalities and viewpoints. Each pure reasoning sample requires connecting multiple relevant clues to support the conclusion. Sample construction combines VLM-based generation, cross-model verification, and human review, involving over 800 person-hours of manual effort. The Position Spatial Judgment (PSJ) task is fully human-annotated, and all test samples undergo human review. The benchmark supports multiple-choice evaluation on ten tasks and open-ended detection, grounding, and counting, assessing both answer selection and direct quantitative prediction. We further develop UAV-PUR, a unified adaptation baseline initialized from pretrained Qwen3-VL models~ qwen3 at the 4B and 8B scales. Its three-stage training comprises perception adaptation, joint capability learning, and final consolidation with language-generation supervision alone. During the first two stages, we introduce three auxiliary heads to provide additional geometric and numerical supervision, helping align visual representations with UAV task requirements. At inference, all tasks use only the original language modeling head. We evaluate 22 general-purpose VLMs on Drone-PUR. Within the same model family, larger models generally achieve stronger performance across the three capability dimensions (Fig.~ fig_1 (b)). However, most models still struggle with PSJ and multi-view reasoning (MVR) (Fig.~ fig_1 (c)). Spatial judgment does not improve consistently with model scale, and models exhibit systematic directional preferences in their predictions. Analyses of relationships across tasks and dimensions show a strong correlation between perception and reasoning across models ( ). Single-task fine-tuning further reveals selective bidirectional transfer: learning to discover and interpret clues can improve reasoning, while training on clue integration tasks can, in turn, enhance perception. Clue masking and modality/view ablations highlight the importance of essential local clues and complementary observations for reasoning. UAV-PUR improves performance across all three dimensions, particularly in target matching and multi-source grounding. Its 4B and 8B variants raise overall multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points over their pretrained counterparts, respectively. UAV-PUR still trails the best-performing API model on pure reasoning tasks, while fine-grained spatial interpretation, reliable open-ended prediction, and cross-source clue integration remain challenging. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce Drone-PUR, a UAV dataset and benchmark organized around a perception--understanding--reasoning framework defined by the roles of visual clues. Its training and evaluation resources for 11 tasks support systematic assessment and domain adaptation. We investigate relationships among UAV visual capabilities through model evaluation, single-task fine-tuning, and ablations. These analyses reveal strong perception--reasoning associations, selective bidirectional capability transfer, and the importance of local clues in reasoning. We assess the benefits of UAV-domain adaptation using UAV-PUR, a baseline combining staged fine-tuning with auxiliary supervision. Joint training across tasks improves all three capability dimensions while revealing persistent limitations in reasoning and spatial understanding. Related Work Vision--Language Tasks and Benchmarks in UAV Scenes Compared with general imagery, UAV scenes often contain smaller targets, less discernible attributes, and more variable viewing geometry, motivating dedicated datasets for aerial perception. Earlier UAV benchmarks~ visdrone,uavdt,HIT-UAV evaluate vision models' ability to detect small objects under varying conditions. UAVScenes~ uavscenes provides image and LiDAR annotations for UAV semantic segmentation. Language-conditioned benchmarks further examine whether models can associate visual details with fine-grained descriptions and contextual relations. RefDrone~ sun2026refdrone and SkyFind~ wang2026skyfind study referring expression grounding~ PSRN, CPGR in UAV scenes, where small objects, scale variations, and clutter complicate target identification. DVGBench~ DVGBench introduces grounding queries that require scene-specific knowledge and inference. UAV-SVG~ UAV-SVG extends visual grounding to targets across aerial video frames. These tasks emphasize the alignment of linguistic descriptions with local visual details, contextual relationships, and target identity. Drone-PUR organizes four grounding settings and evaluates single-image, temporal, cross-view, and joint RGB--TIR grounding within a unified capability framework. VLMs broaden UAV evaluation from visual perception to scene understanding, spatial intelligence, and planning. MM-UAVBench~ Mm-uavbench assesses perception, cognition, and planning in UAV scenarios, while UAVBench~ UAVIT-1M covers image-level and region-level vision--language tasks. UAVQA-Bench~ UAVQA-Bench evaluates UAV image understanding through multiple-choice and visual grounding tasks. UrbanVideo-Bench~ urbanvideo assesses spatiotemporal understanding in videos. Other benchmarks investigate spatial understanding and three-dimensional spatial relations~ SpatialSky,open3d,SpatialUAV , or mathematical reasoning~ AVI-Math . SpatialSky~ SpatialSky evaluates environmental perception and scene understanding using data from UAVScenes~ uavscenes . Collaborative perception and cross-view alignment are also examined through multi-drone observations and paired UAV--satellite inputs~ Aircopbench,LinkS2,Urbench . Alongside these efforts to evaluate UAV capabilities, Drone-PUR explicitly defines reasoning as connecting visual clues through logical inference to support an answer. title: WorldBridge: Bridging Video and Action for Task Generalization in World Action Models
comment: Authors are listed in alphabetical order. Project page: https://worldbridge-jd.github.io/
summary: Achieving the broad task generalization of embodied models in physical environments remains a central challenge in robot learning. We study this challenge in World Action Models (WAMs) through two complementary capabilities: video generalization, which predicts the visual evolution of new tasks, and action generalization, which translates these predictions into executable behavior through a video-to-action bridge. By varying video and action supervision for tasks outside an initial training set, we examine their respective contributions to task transfer. On RoboTwin 2.0, using only in-distribution video-action supervision yields a 25.07% success rate on out-of-distribution tasks. Introducing videos of these tasks without their action labels raises success to 55.90%, while adding just one action-labeled demonstration per task further improves it to 70.70%. These findings suggest that broader video coverage enables task transfer by leveraging existing inverse-dynamics capabilities, while even sparse action supervision further strengthens those capabilities. Guided by this perspective, we introduce WorldBridge, a WAM with separate video and action experts connected through structured attention and trained with joint flow matching. WorldBridge incorporates visual memory at two temporal scales and action forcing, alongside a unified data processing pipeline that standardizes and filters heterogeneous robot trajectories and egocentric hand-derived supervision. Across multiple manipulation benchmarks, WorldBridge achieves state-of-the-art performance among the compared methods, including 96.23% on RoboTwin 2.0 full data setting and 80.9% on clean to random setting, 82.8% on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6% on DOMINO Level-1. Our study highlights the complementary roles of video prediction and action grounding in developing robots that generalize across tasks.
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction Task generalization marks a fundamental shift from earlier pretrained NLP models, such as BERT~ devlin2019bert , to modern large language models (LLMs)~ brown2020language,yang2025qwen3,deepseekai2024v3 . Whereas earlier models typically require task-specific fine-tuning, a single LLM can perform diverse tasks specified through natural-language instructions or a few in-context examples, without updating its parameters for each new task. This capability has motivated the pursuit of generalist embodied agents that can translate human instructions into a broad repertoire of physical behaviors. Vision-language-action (VLA) models represent an important step toward this goal, transferring knowledge from large-scale vision-language pretraining into robot control~ brohan2023rt2, physicalintelligence2025pi05 . However, understanding an instruction does not automatically provide the physical competence needed to execute it. Bringing task generalization into robotics requires connecting semantic knowledge to the visual dynamics and motor behaviors of physical interaction. Despite substantial progress, a prominent focus of embodied generalization research remains robustness to changes in the conditions under which a task is performed, including object arrangements, camera viewpoints, lighting, and visual appearance. Benchmarks such as LIBERO-Plus systematically evaluate these variations, exposing the brittleness of otherwise successful policies~ fei2026liberoplus . Task generalization introduces an additional challenge: a robot must execute behaviors beyond those covered by its original training tasks. Achieving this capability requires understanding how a newly requested task should unfold and producing the actions that realize it, even when corresponding robot demonstrations are scarce or unavailable. World Action Models (WAMs) provide a promising foundation for addressing this challenge by coupling visual prediction with action generation. Video offers dense supervision of physical interactions, allowing models to learn how scenes evolve beyond the coverage of action-labeled robot data. DreamZero demonstrates that video priors can support unseen-task execution and transfer from video-only demonstrations~ ye2026dreamzero , while Zero-WAM explores task generalization through in-context human video guidance~ zhou2026zerowam . Recent advances in native video-action pretraining~ zhang2026native , systematic WAM pretraining~ wang2026openwam , and temporal context~ huang2026longwam further strengthen this paradigm. These developments motivate a more specific question: how do broader video coverage and additional action supervision contribute to task generalization, and when does the connection between them become the limiting factor? In this work, we investigate task generalization in WAMs through two complementary capabilities: video generalization and action generalization . Video generalization enables a model to predict the visual evolution required by tasks beyond its initial training distribution. Action generalization refers to the ability to translate those visual predictions into executable actions beyond the tasks that supplied action supervision. This translation forms a video-to-action bridge, serving the role of an inverse dynamics model (IDM). A model may predict an appropriate visual future yet lack the action grounding needed to realize it. Conversely, a transferable bridge can allow knowledge acquired from additional videos to improve task execution without corresponding action labels, which motivates studying the availability of video and action supervision separately. Figure~ fig:task_generalization illustrates this progression, which we examine by varying supervision for tasks outside an initial in-distribution (ID) training set. With only ID video-action pairs, the model achieves nontrivial but limited generalization, obtaining a 25.07 success rate on out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks. Adding videos of those OOD tasks while keeping action supervision restricted to the ID set increases OOD success to 55.90 . This improvement suggests that expanded video coverage can support new task execution through a bridge learned from ID action supervision. Keeping the video set fixed, adding only one action-labeled demonstration per OOD task further raises success to 70.70 . These rapid gains are consistent with sparse paired examples strengthening the bridge for visual transitions that are already covered by the video data. Together, these observations support a complementary account of task generalization: video supervision expands the range of task evolutions a WAM can model, while action supervision improves its ability to turn that knowledge into reliable control. Guided by this perspective, we introduce WorldBridge, a WAM that couples video prediction and action generation through a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture~ liang2024mot . WorldBridge maintains separate video and action experts trained with a joint flow-matching objective. A structured attention mask establishes a directional information path from observed context to future video representations and then to action predictions, making predicted visual dynamics an explicit source of conditioning for control. Short-term and long-term visual memories provide information about local motion and task progression. We additionally employ action forcing, assigning independent noise levels to actions within a chunk during training so that the action expert learns to predict actions using temporal context at varying levels of corruption. To support learning across heterogeneous sources, we develop a unified pretraining data pipeline for robot trajectories and egocentric human demonstrations. The pipeline standardizes control semantics and maps available robot controls and human hand-derived targets into a shared 46-dimensional action representation. Dimension-wise validity masks preserve partial supervision across embodiments with different control interfaces. Robot trajectories undergo kinematic and temporal consistency checks, while egocentric hand trajectories are standardized in a common reference frame and filtered using geometric and motion constraints. This processing supports broader visual coverage together with usable action supervision, providing a common interface for learning the video-to-action bridge across diverse data sources. Our evaluations demonstrate strong performance across a range of manipulation tasks. WorldBridge achieves state-of-the-art results among the compared methods on multiple benchmarks, with average success rates of 96.23 on RoboTwin 2.0, 80.9 in the RoboTwin 2.0 C2R setting, 82.8 on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6 on DOMINO Level-1. On RMBench, it matches the best result in our comparison, with an 83.0 success rate. We further conduct real-world evaluations on the Agibot-G2 and AC-1 platforms, covering long-horizon execution, memory-dependent tasks, spatial localization, and bimanual coordination. Together with our task-generalization study, these results support the value of jointly developing video prediction and action grounding. Our contributions are threefold: We study task generalization in WAMs through the complementary roles of video generalization and action generalization, quantifying the gains from additional task videos and sparse action supervision. We introduce WorldBridge and a unified data processing pipeline that connect visual dynamics to executable control across heterogeneous robot and egocentric demonstrations. We evaluate WorldBridge across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, RMBench, DOMINO Level-1, SimplerEnv-WidowX, and RoboDojo, covering diverse manipulation demands and distribution shifts. We further deploy it on AgiBot G2 and ARX AC-1, fine-tuning the same jointly pretrained checkpoint for each platform and evaluating long-horizon execution, memory-dependent interaction, spatial alignment, and bimanual coordination. title: CaPtain: A Pipeline for Post-Training Code-as-Policy Robot Agents
summary: Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it. Code-as-policy (CaP) casts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply. Yet existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware. We first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, then apply multi-turn RL. Multi-turn RL must credit tens of agent requests, whose physical effects often surface turns later, from a single end-of-episode outcome. We therefore introduce a physical critic that reads privileged simulator state, never seen by the policy, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success. Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B reaches 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points). Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. We release all code, data, and model weights.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Language-model agents have improved rapidly in coding, web navigation, and tool use, and much of this progress follows a common recipe: the agent acts inside a fixed execution harness, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teaches it the interface, and multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) refines its behavior from the outcomes of its own interactions~ katcoder2026,uitars2,sao2026,feng2025gigpo . Code-as-policy (CaP) agents~ liang2023cap,huang2023voxposer,qin2026agenticrobots give robot manipulation the same form: the policy observes camera images, writes programs against perception and motion APIs, and reads back what happened. Since the program is composed at test time, a CaP agent inherits much of the generalization of the language model that writes it, and frontier models have made this approach strikingly capable. Used directly as a robot policy, GPT-6 Astra ranks above every public entry on the RoboDojo leaderboard~ astra2026robodojo , and with a coding harness it solves 94.0 of LIBERO-PRO episodes~ pyrualean2026 . This raises a natural question: Can a small open model be trained into such a CaP agent with the same SFT-and-RL recipe, rather than relying on a frontier model at test time? In practice, existing CaP agents sidestep training, and in doing so hand the manipulation itself to components the agent cannot learn to improve. One line of work prompts closed frontier models without weight updates~ openrua2026,racap2026,waa2026,aspire2026,k1harness2026 . These systems come with high finical cost of calling frontier models in each episode~ openrua2026,racap2026,waa2026 , cannot be fine-tuned for new robots or tasks, and cannot run on onboard compute. Another line delegates manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) or high-level skills. PyRUA trains a 4B coder over a frozen VLA and a motion planner~ pyrualean2026 , AgenticRoboRL trains a planner around a frozen LIBERO-trained VLA~ agenticroborl2026 , SenseNova-RoboRSI builds a 27B agent around reusable skills and optional VLA calls~ sensenovaroborsi2026 , and Gemini 4 Argon exposes code-as-policies through skills such as grasp and place~ argon2026robotics . In these systems, the code decides which skill to call, but the skill decides how to grasp, approach, and place. Therefore, the agent stays bounded by the data on which the skill was trained, and RL can at best learn to sequence it. Small open vision-language models (VLMs), meanwhile, fail outright when asked to control a robot directly. Qwen3.5-4B solves none of the LIBERO episodes in our harness, and the few efforts that train such models rely mainly on SFT~ guava2026 or single-turn text-only RL~ fu2026capx . What is missing is a complete SFT-and-RL recipe that teaches a small open VLM to manipulate through low-level primitives, with every manipulation decision made by the policy itself. Applying the recipe at this low level is harder than at the skill level, for a reason that does not arise for language agents. Without semantic skills such as grasp and place, the policy must itself decide where to grasp, from which direction to approach, and when to close the gripper, and these decisions are spread over tens of requests per episode, most of which only perceive or verify. Multi-turn RL must then credit these requests, whose physical effects often surface several turns later, with a single outcome observed only at the end of the episode. Outcome-only RL assigns the same credit to every request, while a language-model critic would have to infer physical progress indirectly from text and images. Robot learning, however, offers an asymmetry that language agents lack: training runs in simulation, where exact object poses, grasp states, and sub-goal progress are known, even though the deployed policy must act from its cameras alone. A critic can thus read the physical state that the policy cannot see, and credit each request by how much it moves the task toward success, while the policy itself still acts from its cameras at test time. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline built on these two observations. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, an execution environment that exposes 22 low-level perception, geometric measurement, and guarded-motion primitives and nothing higher. There are no grasp, place, or open-drawer skills and no VLA. Perception returns masks and points, and motion takes an explicit end-effector pose or gripper command. Every call returns a structured text receipt reporting what physically happened, such as measured poses, contact forces, or why a motion stopped, and the policy-facing API is unchanged across LIBERO~ liu2023libero , RoboTwin~2.0~ robotwin2 , RoboDojo~ robodojo2026 , SimplerEnv~ simplerenv2024 , CaP-Bench~ fu2026capx , and a physical robot. We first apply SFT on in-harness trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, rendered in exactly the multi-turn format the policy sees at deployment. We then run multi-turn RL with a simulator critic that reads privileged physical state hidden from the policy and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success, combining the streaming RL formulation of SAO~ sao2026 with asymmetric actor-critic training~ pinto2017asymmetric . Since this change is measured at a fixed time index, requests that only perceive or verify receive near-zero credit, and credit concentrates on grasps and placements. The critic is used only during training. At test time, the policy relies on camera images and receipts alone. Applying CaPtain to Qwen3.5-4B yields CaPtain-4B, which raises the held-out LIBERO success from 0 to 55.4 after SFT and to 73.8 after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, CaPtain-4B reaches 78.5 , above frontier-model agents such as K1~ k1harness2026 (77.2 ), WAA~ waa2026 (75.6 ), and ASPIRE~ aspire2026 (71.7 ). RL also gains more when it acts on low-level primitives: across the four LIBERO-PRO suites it adds 19.4 points to our SFT model, whereas RL over a frozen VLA adds 5.9 points in AgenticRoboRL~ agenticroborl2026 , although the two start from different baselines. These gains persist under perturbation, ranging from +17.6 to +21.2 points across LIBERO-PRO~ liberopro2025 , LIBERO-Plus~ liberoplus2025 , and LIBERO-MAX~ liberomax2026 , with all seven LIBERO-Plus perturbation dimensions improving significantly; by contrast, reported results for end-to-end policies show ~ pi05 falling from 97 on LIBERO to 12.8 on LIBERO-PRO~ liberopro2025 and the RL-tuned RIPT-VLA~ riptvla scoring no higher than its base model on LIBERO-Plus~ liberoplus2025 . Without target-domain training, CaPtain-4B reaches 83.3 on SimplerEnv WidowX, scores 75.0 on CaP-Bench, above frontier models and a 7B coder trained with RL on that benchmark, and completes tasks on a physical robot after adaptation in a coarse simulated twin alone. Transfer remains limited on RoboTwin~2.0 and RoboDojo (22.6 and 0.8 success), which require dual-arm coordination and unfamiliar arm kinematics. Together, these results suggest that robot manipulation over a low-level execution harness can be post-trained like any other language agent. Contributions. CaPtain, an open, end-to-end SFT-and-RL pipeline that turns a small open VLM into a standalone CaP agent. We release the SFT data, the training code and the CaPtain-4B weights. CaPtain-Harness, a portable execution harness with low-level primitives only, exposing 22 perception, measurement, and guarded-motion capabilities with grounded text receipts. A simulator critic for multi-turn VLM agents that converts privileged physical state transitions into dense per-request credit, with analyses showing that credit concentrates on physical manipulation decisions. A comprehensive evaluation showing that RL gains persist across three perturbation suites, that a 4B policy surpasses several frontier-model agents at a small fraction of their cost, and that it transfers zero-shot across benchmarks and embodiments and to a physical robot without real-world data. Related Work sec:related Code-as-policy robot agents. title: From Teleoperation to Long-Horizon Dexterity: Evaluating Visuomotor Skills and Offline Proxies for Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Imitation learning policies are intended to make robotic manipulation robust to variations in object pose, appearance, and environment that challenge pre-programmed motion. However, real-world performance remains difficult to predict, as conventional optimization signals such as validation loss show no consistent relationship with robot success. To identify the design choices that govern real-world performance, 281 imitation-learning policies spanning seven policy families were evaluated in approximately 1,700 real-robot trials of RJ45 connector grasping and insertion using a five-fingered robotic hand. Controlled ablations showed that observation and action representations dominated conventional optimizer and sampling choices. For point-cloud policies, region-of-interest cropping, representation in the robot-base frame, and normalization within the point encoder each improved success by 70-100 percentage points. For the vision-language-action policy, absolute rather than relative action prediction improved insertion success by up to 70 percentage points. Skill decomposition, multi-view perception, and recovery demonstrations were associated with the strongest-performing systems, although their effects were not independently isolated. Of 67 offline metrics evaluated, only five measures of predicted-motion smoothness and directness reliably correlated with insertion success (r = -0.70 to -0.80), and only within a single policy family. These results identify representation choices as key determinants of real-world imitation-learning performance and show that offline metrics can shortlist policies, but cannot replace real-robot evaluation.

Introduction Imitation learning offers a practical route to robotic manipulation that generalises across the variations in object pose, appearance and environment that defeat pre-programmed motion, learning a direct observation-to-action mapping from demonstrations rather than hand-engineered controllers~ argall2009survey,zhao2023act,chi2024diffusion . Recent visuomotor policies including diffusion and flow-based action generators, transformer decoders, and large vision-language-action models, have driven rapid progress on real single-arm tasks~ chi2024diffusion,zhao2023act,black2024pi0 . Yet the paradigm inherits well-known liabilities: behavioral cloning accumulates error under co-variate shift~ ross2011dagger , and real-world success remains hard to predict because conventional offline signals such as validation loss correlate weakly, or not at all, with task performance~ mandlekar2021matters . As a result, the design choices that govern a policy, like observation and action representations, encoder pretraining, sampling and optimization, are typically settled by expensive real-robot trials, and systematic evidence to guide them is scarce, especially for the dexterous, contact-rich skills demanded by multi-fingered hands~ florence2021implicit,openai2020dexterous . We study these questions on a representative contact-rich task: inserting an RJ45 cable connector, which demands millimetre precision on a deformable object where small changes in cable pose or grasp break fixed trajectories and still challenge end-to-end learned policies~ chi2024diffusion,ze2024dp3,black2024pi0 . We decompose the task into four stages: two moves between known poses handled by classical motion, and two learned contact-rich skills, grasp and insert (Section~ sec:system ). We ask how best to build those skills for a five-fingered hand. We contribute (i)~a real-robot ablation study that isolates individual policy components (data augmentation, image-encoder pretraining, action representation, point-cloud reference frame (camera or robot base), cropping and normalization, prediction horizon, optimizer, denoising sampler and policy family) and reports for every comparison all training settings that changed between the two runs; and (ii)~a leak-free test of whether offline metrics can stand in for robot trials. System and Protocol sec:system Preliminaries. Every policy we compare maps the current observation and robot state to a short chunk of future actions, differing along three axes. Observation encoder: Diffusion Policy (DP)~ chi2024diffusion and ACT~ zhao2023act encode RGB images; DP3~ ze2024dp3 encodes a point cloud with a small PointNet; and iDP3~ ze2024idp3 applies a multi-stage point encoder to egocentric clouds. Action generator: DP, DP3 and iDP3 denoise the action chunk, flow matching~ lipman2023flow instead regresses a velocity field, ACT decodes the chunk with a conditional-autoencoder transformer, and an equivariant diffusion policy~ yang2024equibot bakes rotation and scale symmetry into its point encoder. Pretraining: these policies are trained on our demonstrations, at most with an ImageNet- or R3M-initialised image encoder, whereas the vision-language-action (VLA) model ~ pi05,black2024pi0 is pretrained on large cross-embodiment data and finetuned with LoRA~ hu2022lora . We selected these policies as widely used, open-source methods with strong reported results on real single-arm manipulation from RGB or depth input. Comparable ablations are typically confined to simulation or parallel-jaw grippers, and cable manipulation has largely relied on engineered pipelines~ zhu2023cable . Setup. An RJ45 cable connector sits in a socket on one of two grasp jigs, at the centre or left of the work area, while a third jig holds the target socket. Each trial proceeds in four stages (Appendix~ app:setup ): (1)~classical motion to a preset start pose at the jig holding the cable, which FoundationPose~ wen2024foundationpose identifies; (2)~a learned policy grasps the connector and pulls it from its socket; (3)~classical motion carries it to the insert jig; and (4)~a learned policy inserts it. Demonstrations are teleoperated on a Franka Research~3 arm with a Tesollo DG5F-M hand at 30\,Hz; policies run at 10\,Hz, since 10\,Hz replay reproduced the outcomes of 30\,Hz replay. Policies observe a wrist RGB-D camera, and two-view variants add a static third-person camera; codebases and settings are in Appendix~ app:policies . Scoring. Each trial is scored by the last stage the robot completed: Fail ( , the hand did not close on the connector), Grasp ( , it closed but never reached the grip threshold needed to lift), Pick ( , pulled out but not seated) or Insert ( , seated in the target socket). An inserted trial was therefore also picked, so over trials Pick , Insert pick and Insert , pooled per checkpoint with 95 Clopper--Pearson intervals; the rates of two policies that differ by one change are compared with Fisher's exact test. Ablation Results Paired comparisons. Fig.~ fig:results a compares pairs of policies that differ in one component (isolated) or, where marked, several; Appendix~ app:changes lists every change tested, and rates are percentages of all pooled trials (Appendix~ app:protocol ). Among isolated changes, a region-of-interest (ROI) crop raised the iDP3 pick rate from 0 to 100 , and applying PointNet's layer normalisation after every hidden layer, rather than only to its output, raised DP3 insertion from 0 to 70 . Predicting absolute instead of relative actions raised the two-view insert from 30 to 100 with the 6D rotation representation~ zhou2019continuity , but only from 89 to 100 with Euler angles. On the same balanced dataset (Appendix~ app:data ), the robot-base frame raised PointNet picks from 20 to 100 , with a second pair on other clouds showing the same trend. Recovery episodes alone raised the iDP3 pipeline from 50 to 80 , which is not significant at this . The largest gains came from several changes at once. A second camera view together with recovery episodes (Appendix~ app:data ), on a balanced set re-drawn from the two-camera recordings (180 episodes plus 108 recovery episodes, against 186), raised the insert from 0 to 100 , while a second view with a larger UNet and no ImageNet initialisation raised the RGB DP insert from 70 to 100 on the same data. Every grasp-and-insert policy inserted in at most 10 of trials, whereas the best decomposed pipelines inserted in every trial, and the decomposed pipeline with recovery episodes rose from 0 to 50 . The split is therefore consistently associated with insertion, though its effect is never isolated from other changes. Second-order factors. No visual augmentation improved the RGB grasp skill's pick rate over the unaugmented baseline (40 ). ImageNet initialisation helped grasping, most notably at the left jig, but not insertion, where pretrained and from-scratch backbones each inserted 50--70 . And none of fifteen perturbations of the iDP3 grasp skill (optimiser, width, depth, DPM-Solver++~ lu2022dpmpp , -prediction~ salimans2022progressive ) clearly beat the defaults. Families, cost and robustness. In Table~ tab:family , iDP3, and a two-view DP insert pipeline achieve insertion in every trial, RGB DP and PointNet DP3 in 70 , and the best flow-matching and ACT pipelines in 30--50 , while most PointNet DP3 and ACT pairings never inserted. The compact point-cloud skill matches the VLA at an eighth of its inference memory. The iDP3 pipeline retained 80--100 of its insertions under changed lighting, background, site and sunlight; only a tighter-tolerance socket broke it (0--40 ; Table~ tab:app-robust ). Offline Metrics as Proxies for Robot Trials For every checkpoint with robot trials we computed 67 metrics on validation episodes held out from its own training set (list, selection criteria and loss curves in Appendix~ app:offline , Fig.~ fig:app-loss ) and asked whether any tracked the checkpoint's robot success rate. Each cell of Fig.~ fig:results b correlates one metric within one group of policy families and one jig set (centre only or both). A cell is reliable only if its correlation survives correction for multiple testing and keeps its sign when any single policy is removed. No cell passed for the centre-only checkpoints or for groups mixing RGB and point-cloud policies, whose correlations were weak or sign-flipped depending on the policies included, so these metrics cannot compare policy types. Only for the 21 iDP3 insert checkpoints tested at both jigs did five of the 67 pass, all negative ( to ): lower values inserted more often. The five describe the predicted end-effector path over 50 frames per validation episode (mean speed, path length, path-length ratio, jerk and spectral power), so all are low when the path is short, direct and smooth. A policy whose predictions jitter frame to frame traces a long, jerky path that appears on the robot as hovering and misalignment at the socket. Because the five correlate strongly with each other ( -- ), they carry the same information and act as a single smoothness score that can rank a family's insert checkpoints before robot testing. No metric tracked the pick rate, plausibly because grasp failures arise at first contact, which replayed observations do not reproduce. title: Confidence-Modulated Safety Filtering for End-to-End Policies
summary: End-to-end policies, from task-specific controllers to robot foundation models, learn complex behavior from raw observations but are not guaranteed to remain safe, so they are often wrapped in a safety filter. The resulting system operates under two domains: the filter's operational design domain (ODD), where its assumptions hold and safety is certified, and the policy's competence domain, where it is reliable. Filters typically fix their conservativeness regardless of the policy's competence, trading performance inside the ODD against margin beyond it. We ask whether the policy's confidence should set that level, and propose a filter-agnostic pipeline that modulates it at runtime: inside the ODD, where every setting is safe, confidence buys performance; beyond it, low confidence adds margin, which helps when it flags where the filter's model fails. Preliminary F1TENTH simulations, where this holds, show the modulated filter combining the strengths of permissive and conservative filters.

Introduction sec:intro End-to-end policies that map observations directly to actions have become a practical route to capable autonomous decision-making, from task-specific controllers~ bojarski2016end,kaufmann2023champion,geles2024demonstrating to generalist robot foundation models~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2025pi0 . Trained on enough data, they often perform well and, much of the time, act safely. But not always: their competence is tied to the domain of the inputs they were trained on, and away from it their behavior is unspecified. A racing policy that drives a familiar track flawlessly may steer into a wall once the lighting changes or the tires lose grip~ filos2020can,dehaan2019causal . Worse, such failures arrive without warning: the policy issues an action exactly as it always does, and nothing in its action signals that it has left the regime in which its behavior was learned~ hecker2018failure,agia2024unpacking . A standard remedy for safety-critical deployment is to wrap the policy in a safety filter that monitors its proposed actions and overrides them when they threaten to drive the system into failure~ hsu2024safety,borquez2024safety,ames2019control . A safety filter, however, is only as good as the assumptions behind it. Its certificate rests on a model of the world, such as the system dynamics, a map of free space, a bound on disturbances, and holds only within the operational design domain (ODD) where those assumptions are met. Inside the ODD, the filter keeps the system safe regardless of the policy it guards; beyond it, the filter keeps acting, but nothing is guaranteed~ hsu2024safety,sae2021j3016 . The learned policy has its own competence domain, the conditions under which its training makes its behavior reliable. The two domains do not need to coincide, yet standard safety-filtered pipelines treat the policy as an arbitrary black box and ignore whether it is operating within its competence domain~ wabersich2023data,wabersich2021predictive . Blind to the policy's competence, standard filters commit to a single level of conservativeness, set by design parameters such as a barrier decay rate or a safety-value threshold~ bansal2017hamilton,alan2022safe . Inside the ODD every setting is safe, but a conservative filter overrides a competent policy early and often, eroding its performance, while a permissive one lets an unreliable policy reach the boundary of the safe set, where abrupt fallback interventions are costly~ hu2022sharp,hu2024active . Beyond the ODD, losing the certificate does not make failure inevitable: the filter becomes an imperfect one, and its conservativeness sets a margin that may or may not translate into safety. On a race track, a wide margin may save a car whose filter assumes dry asphalt once the track turns wet, yet it also brakes the car on straights the policy has driven thousands of times. Whatever value is chosen is fixed and spent uniformly, whether or not the policy has proven reliable there. A fixed conservativeness has been questioned before, with adaptation driven by performance~ parwana2025rate,kim2025learning,kim2025adapt , by the filter's own prediction errors~ huriot2026safe , or by the policy's own uncertainty, which can tighten a CBF filter~ yu2025uncertainty,li2026risk or trigger a switch to a fallback when inputs look novel~ richter2017safe . Building on this line of work, we ask whether the task policy's confidence should set a safety filter's conservativeness: a confidence monitor estimates how much the task policy can be trusted on the current input and sets the filter's conservativeness (Fig.~ fig:pipeline ). When confidence is high, the policy is likely reliable and the filter steps back; when it is low, the policy's behavior is unpredictable and conservativeness costs little, provided that low confidence signals risk. Inside the ODD, safety is untouched, since every setting is certified, and modulation only buys performance; beyond it, modulation adds margin where the policy is less trustworthy. We give a filter-agnostic formulation, for any confidence measure and any filter whose conservativeness can be graded, and use the two domains to make explicit what modulation buys inside and beyond the ODD, and under which conditions. title: STAR: Steering Action Representations during Inference
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions, showing strong capabilities across robotic manipulation tasks. However, in our probing experiment, we find that action representations near the action output do not fully preserve task-relevant visual grounding. Motivated by this late-layer grounding gap, we introduce STAR, for STeering Action Representations, a training-free inference method for pre-trained VLAs. STAR applies an exponential moving average over late-layer residual updates, allowing later action representations to inherit object-aware update directions from earlier layers without model updates or architectural changes. It further uses recent proprioceptive states to adapt the mixing strength, using conservative mixing when execution dynamics change rapidly. Experiments on robot manipulation benchmarks show that STAR improves late-layer object awareness and increases average task success rates by 4.0 percentage points. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/STAR.

Introduction sec:introduction Despite the tremendous success of vision-language models (VLMs)~ llava,molmo,prismatic,eaglevlm,paligemma,qwen3 , previous work has shown that they may overly rely on language priors, producing responses that are not fully grounded in the visual input~ pope,vcd,opera,m3id,damo . Meanwhile, recent studies also observe that vision-language-action models (VLAs) exhibit similar behavior patterns, such as insufficient use of task-relevant visual cues~ reconvla,gaze_regularized_vla,obeyed_vla,pointvla,coavla or distraction from irrelevant visual tokens~ dtp,cgvd,tag,cogvla . Inspired by these works, we ask a key question: how strongly are action representations in VLAs grounded in task-relevant visual evidence ? To probe the dependence of action representations on visual evidence, we design a controlled experiment. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:motivation (a), we mask the target object pixels by replacing them with the mean RGB values of the image. By masking the visual information important for action execution, we expect the action representations to differ from those produced without interference. To measure the representation change induced by object masking, we define an object awareness score, computed as . Here, is the hidden state of the -th layer in Figure~ fig:motivation (b), while and denote the original and masked observations, respectively. This metric provides a heuristic estimate of how strongly task-relevant visual evidence affects the action representation. A larger score indicates a larger difference in the representation after masking. The resulting object-awareness score for ~ pi05 is reported in Figure~ fig:motivation (c). We find that, during native inference, object awareness increases through early-to-middle layers and drops in late layers. This suggests that visual evidence is gradually aggregated into action representations from early to middle layers, but fades away in late layers. This probing experiment demonstrates a grounding gap in late layers during VLA inference. To address the gap, we introduce , for STeering Action Representations, a training-free method that regularizes the action representations in late layers without updating model weights. Intuitively, steers late-layer action representations by carrying residual updates from earlier layers to later layers. Specifically, applies an exponential moving average (EMA)~ ema over late-layer updates. When action semantics change rapidly, such as during end-effector rotation or fine-grained adjustment, the intervention should be conservative. Conversely, when the robot does not rotate, such as when moving in a straight line, the intervention can be stronger. These differences in execution dynamics are reflected in recent proprioceptive trajectories. In short, uses a proprioception-modulated EMA to smooth cross-layer residual updates, carrying object-aware directions from earlier layers. This design is validated through our object awareness measurement and robotic manipulation benchmarks. title: AVID: A Weakly Aligned RGB-Infrared Dataset and Perturbation Benchmark for Tiny Aerial Targets
summary: Long-range detection of small drones is complicated by their visual similarity to birds and by the limited detail available from ground-based cameras. Combining visible and infrared observations offers complementary information, but their usefulness depends on target size, cross-modal alignment, and image quality. We present AVID, a benchmark for studying these factors using real RGB-infrared bird-drone surveillance footage originating from the Drone Detection Dataset and curated for the IEEE ICIP 2025 Video and Image Processing Cup. AVID comprises 32,040 corresponding frame pairs from 115 videos, with 35,952 existing bird and drone annotations at $320\times256$ resolution. Targets occupy an unusually narrow size range: 68.1\% have a geometric-mean bounding-box side of 8--16 pixels, and 99.0\% meet the COCO small-object criterion. To characterize the geometric difficulty of combining the modalities, we introduce an object-relative alignment ratio and an alignment burden curve. In a sample of 300 frame pairs, 32.3\% have estimated global translations greater than 5 pixels; among the 264 pairs with matching annotations, 16.3\% exceed one median target side. We further introduce AVID-C, which simulates seven families of image degradation at five severity levels independently in RGB, infrared, or both. A fixed-feature analysis examines how scale, degradation, and added cross-modal shifts affect fitted bird-drone class overlap. At 12--16 pixels, the Bhattacharyya error bounds are 0.148 for RGB, 0.198 for infrared, and 0.046 for their combined features. These values describe separation in the specified feature and density models, not detector accuracy. Together, AVID and AVID-C support scale-aware, alignment-aware, and sensor-specific studies of tiny aerial targets.

At this scale, the silhouette and texture that distinguish a drone from a bird are often poorly resolved, while background clutter, blur, and sensor noise can dominate the target appearance. Recognition is therefore difficult not only because the objects are small, but because their class-specific visual information is easily lost. Prior work has addressed bird-drone classification selvi2022deep , drone localization and tracking 10193217,10328384 , and multimodal drone localization 11700652 . A complementary question concerns the observations themselves: how much class information remains when targets are tiny, the camera views are displaced, or one sensor is degraded? Visible and infrared imagery offer different views of the same aerial target. RGB captures appearance and scene context, whereas infrared records thermal contrast that may persist under poor visible-light conditions. These benefits are not unconditional. The cameras have different optics and response characteristics, and corresponding frames need not be registered. A shift of five pixels is minor for a large object but substantial for a target whose bounding box is ten pixels wide. Likewise, a perturbation affecting one modality may have a different effect on the other. Consequently, evaluations that report only an aggregate detection score can obscure the conditions under which multisensor observations become useful or unreliable. provides a setting for studying these questions with birds and drones observed by ground-based RGB and infrared cameras. The benchmark comprises 32,040 corresponding frame pairs from 115 surveillance videos and 35,952 annotated instances. Its footage originates from the Drone Detection Dataset of Svanstr\"om and colleagues svanstrom2021multisensor,svanstrom2020repository , with bird-drone observations curated for the IEEE ICIP 2025 Video and Image Processing Cup ieeevipcup2025 . Importantly, correspondence between the RGB and infrared views does not imply pixel-level registration. Rather than treating this discrepancy as incidental, makes it part of the evaluation setting. First, 24,489 annotations (68.1 ) have a geometric-mean bounding-box side of only 8--16 pixels in the native images; 99.0 belong to the COCO small-object category. We therefore examine finer size intervals rather than treating virtually all targets as a single size group. Second, sensor displacement must be interpreted at the scale of these objects. title: Veloxity: Towards Memory-Safe UAV Embedded Firmware using the Rust Programming Language
summary: Recent years have witnessed increased momentum towards memory-safe programming languages for safety-critical systems. Memory-safe languages can eliminate entire classes of common software errors that have historically required extensive analysis and expenditure to avoid. Nevertheless, memory-safe language adoption in aerospace remains fragmented and incomplete, particularly for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Recent Rust UAV projects either run only in simulation, are closed source, or have not been integrated with an established autonomy ecosystem and tested against existing C/C++ firmware. To address this gap, we present Veloxity: an open-source embedded UAV autopilot written in the memory-safe Rust programming language. Veloxity lowers the barrier to using memory-safe languages within modern ecosystems by providing a minimal, modular foundation for autonomous UAVs. We compare Veloxity to equivalent autopilots written in C++ in simulation, with hardware testbenches, and via outdoor waypoint-following flight tests, demonstrating functional parity with improved performance. These results indicate that modern memory-safe languages are a viable option for reliable and performant firmware for autonomous aerospace systems.

In small UAVs, timing-sensitive sensor processing, estimation, control, mixing, and actuator output remain on an embedded flight controller, making the robustness of the embedded firmware paramount. Defects in the firmware (particularly those related to program memory use) can result in loss of vehicle and damage to livelihood. Most open-source flight-control firmware is implemented in C or C++ surveyOfUAVAutopilotsChao2010,surveyOfOpenSourceAutopilots2024 , languages that provide limited compile-time protection against memory errors and unsynchronized shared-state access. Memory-safety violations such as out-of-bounds accesses, use-after-free errors, and data races can corrupt program state or terminate execution. Because their effects may emerge far from the original defect and depend on a particular execution timing, these faults can be difficult to reproduce (and thus difficult to diagnose). In flight firmware, the resulting corruption or loss of execution can affect sensing, state estimation, control, or actuator output while the vehicle is airborne. Preventing such faults largely relies on development practices including coding standards, review, static analysis, and testing. High-assurance languages and toolsets such as Ada and SPARK offer stronger verification, but obtaining that assurance can impose substantial development tradeoffs. It can require developers to define proof obligations, work within language restrictions, and maintain specialized verification expertise. These costs have not prevented the use of Ada and SPARK in high-assurance aerospace software or targeted flight-control demonstrations. For example, Adamant provides a model-based, platform-agnostic Ada framework for embedded spacecraft flight software, including multitasking and support for SPARK proofs adamantFramework . The Crazyflie's stock firmware is written in C bitcraze2026crazyflie , but a separate demonstration rewrote the vehicle's stabilization subsystem in SPARK, proved it free of runtime errors, and flew it with the remaining C drivers and FreeRTOS infrastructure unchanged gracio2015crazyflieSpark . However, the proof effort, specialized expertise, and comparatively small development ecosystem associated with Ada and SPARK can impede widespread adoption in hobbyist and open-source UAV communities, where rapid iteration and integration with existing software are priorities. This leaves room for approaches that balance compile-time protection with rapid development and compatibility with established research ecosystems. Rust rustbook2026borrowing is a modern programming language built to enforce memory access constraints through ownership rules and its type system, while retaining much of the familiar syntax of C/C++. In Rust, memory management can largely be checked and verified at compile time, but maintains execution speeds similar to C/C++ that are required for low-level control and resource-constrained embedded software. These protections do not depend on a garbage collector, and Rust's no std environment supports systems without a conventional operating-system runtime. Rust is also favorable for AI-assisted development due to the detailed compiler diagnostics capabilities that code-generation systems can use to perform iterative development and checking. Perhaps the most compelling motivation Rust provides is the evidence from large companies that these safety benefits do not come with penalties in productivity or development. For instance, in a survey of more than 1,000 Google developers who contributed Rust code (many of whom came from C++), Google found no evidence of lower productivity in Rust relative to the languages those developers had previously used; more than half reported becoming as productive in Rust within four months bergstromBrennan2023rustJourney . Despite the advantages, evidence remains limited for Rust in embedded flight firmware or for its evaluation within an established autonomy ecosystem. Rust has only recently begun to appear in UAV software. Peng pengQuad is a Rust quadrotor framework for simulation, trajectory planning, and control, but does not run on flight hardware. Fusion Reflex fusionReflex is a commercial flight controller whose Linux-hosted software is written in Rust, but it is not open source. Most recently, Cybflight lin2026cybflight runs a modular Rust autopilot for calculating state estimation and nonlinear control directly on an STM32H743 flight controller. None of these, however, operate within an existing ROS~2 macenski2022ros2 autonomy ecosystem or present a comparison against an established C or C++ firmware. To our knowledge, no published literature has compared the use of Rust to more common alternatives in embedded UAV firmware. To overcome this shortcoming, we present the following contributions: An open-source UAV firmware autopilot implementation written in Rust. This includes a novel board- and protocol-independent no std core architecture supporting embedded and simulated runtimes, with a priority-based scheduler that prioritizes high-rate inertial measurement unit (IMU) processing and control. An empirical comparison with the ROSflight firmware (C/C++) it was modeled after at multiple integration boundaries: flash footprint, communication latency, numerical agreement, and SIL waypoint following within the Robot Operating System 2 (ROS~2) ROScopter autonomy stack. A real-time hardware implementation and field demonstration of Veloxity on STM32H743-based Pixracer Pro flight control unit (FCU) commonly used for flight-control research. ROSflight Architecture ROSflight jackson2020rosflight,moore2025rosflight2 is a lean, open-source autopilot ecosystem designed to reduce the effort required to move UAV research from simulation to hardware. It was developed to reduce the barrier to entry for conducting highly customized autopilot research by favoring a modular, documented, and deliberately limited architecture over the broader feature sets of modern autopilots (e.g., PX4 and ArduPilot ardupilot,px4repo ). Veloxity extends the ROSflight ecosystem with memory safe firmware guarantees. The ROSflight autopilot uses the common paradigm of splitting computation between a FCU and a separate onboard computer known as the companion computer. The FCU handles real-time tasks such as low-level sensor aggregation and actuator commands, while the companion computer performs high-level control and planning. Computation on the companion computer is performed within ROS~2. ROS~2 is a middleware that organizes software into nodes, which communicate through topics, services, actions, and parameters macenski2022ros2 . ROS~2 also helps facilitate a MAVLink connection with the FCU. The ROSflight autopilot can also connect to an optional ground station computer, allowing operators to specify high-level goals for the companion computer, manage system parameters, and monitor downlinked telemetry in real time. Within the ROSflight 2.0 architecture on the companion computer, the rosflight io node translates ROS~2 topics and service calls to and from MAVLink messages exchanged with the FCU over a serial connection moore2025rosflight2 . In ROSflight 2.0, the companion-computer flight stack is separated into distinct ROS~2 nodes for estimation, control, navigation, and application logic. For multirotors, these nodes form the ROScopter autonomy stack moore2026roscopter , shown in Fig.~ fig:rosflight_architecture . Below this at the system level, the FCU interfaces directly with sensors, actuators, and the safety pilot's radio-control (RC) receiver. It also manages firmware state and optionally supports the fast estimation and control loops needed for manual or assisted flight. Memory safety is the proper control of memory in computer programs to avoid improper or unexpected access and release brinker2025memorySafety . Traditional systems programming languages (such as C and C++) provide unrestricted access to system resources and rely on programmer discipline to protect against memory-unsafe behavior. While C++ has notably added memory safety features such as smart pointers, taking advantage of all C++ has to offer frequently requires users to integrate their code with unsafe community code DeLozier2024cppCommunitySafety . title: Prior-Guided Single-Exposure HDR Novel View Synthesis via Base-Gain Representation
summary: Single-exposure high dynamic range (HDR) novel view synthesis (NVS) recovers HDR scenes from low dynamic range (LDR) views captured at a single exposure and estimates camera response function (CRF) for LDR re-exposure. Without HDR ground-truth, using single-exposure LDR views as the sole source of direct supervision underconstrains HDR reconstruction and cannot ensure its faithful recovery, motivating the need for learned LDR-to-HDR reconstruction priors. Moreover, single-exposure LDR views supervise CRF only over a limited range, necessitating a learnable prior for reliable re-exposure beyond it. We propose PriorGS, a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that addresses both challenges by (1) guiding HDR recovery with pseudo-HDR supervision from 2D single-exposure HDR reconstruction methods while anchoring it to input LDR views through a closed reconstruction loop; and (2) regularizing CRF modeling with a learnable prior that guarantees monotonicity and promotes plausible responses. Yet cross-view inconsistencies in independently generated pseudo-HDR targets impair scene reconstruction when HDR is encoded directly as Gaussian's color attribute. We therefore introduce a 3D base-gain HDR representation that factors HDR radiance into an LDR base and an overlaid 3D gain field, promoting robustness to such inconsistencies and enabling 3D HDR appearance editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate PriorGS's substantial superiority over baselines.

Introduction sec:intro High dynamic range (HDR) novel view synthesis (NVS) aims to reconstruct a 3D scene's geometry and HDR radiance from multi-view low dynamic range (LDR) observations, with the dual objective of synthesizing novel HDR views and rendering their LDR counterparts at unseen exposures. Compared with conventional LDR-NVS Nerf, GaussianSplats , HDR-NVS represents a wider range of scene illumination, preserving textures in both highlights and shadows. This richer representation improves the visual appeal and realism of reconstructed scenes and benefits many downstream applications photorealistic_rendering, inverse_render, robotics . Most HDR-NVS methods rely on multi-exposure LDR captures HDR_Nerf, HDRGS, GaussHDR that typically require static scenes and tedious acquisition to avoid motion artifacts. Motivated by this limitation, recent methods, including ours, target HDR-NVS with more accessible single-exposure LDR inputs SeHDR, MonoHDR . Also, as calibrated per-view HDR capture is rarely practical, we target HDR recovery without access to HDR ground-truth (GT). HDR scene radiance represents linear scene-referred light over a wide intensity range. During LDR capture, this radiance is converted to sensor exposure, transformed by a nonlinear camera response function (CRF), quantized, and partially lost through highlight clipping and shadow noise EMoR . Recovering HDR radiance from this degraded single-exposure observation is hence fundamentally underconstrained cheat_sihdr , motivating 2D single-exposure HDR reconstruction methods that learn LDR-to-HDR reconstruction priors from large data intrinsic_hdr, single-hdr . The same challenge arises in single-exposure HDR-NVS: using single-exposure views as the only source of direct supervision leaves HDR reconstruction underconstrained and cannot ensure its accurate recovery. This motivates the need for learned LDR-to-HDR reconstruction priors to guide HDR recovery in single-exposure HDR-NVS, a critical factor overlooked by prior works. Figure~ fig:hdr_fail illustrates this: when trained on the same single-exposure inputs, existing methods lacking learned LDR-to-HDR priors reproduce the observed exposure yet recover an incorrect HDR radiance. Our method, however, achieves high-fidelity HDR recovery by leveraging this prior. Beyond high-fidelity HDR recovery, a holistic HDR-NVS method must accurately re-expose HDR radiance to LDR views at unseen exposures through CRF modeling, an objective often bypassed by existing single-exposure methods. Unlike multi-exposure captures that enable supervision for a wide CRF range, single-exposure views supervise only the camera’s limited unsaturated range at one exposure, leaving the CRF unconstrained elsewhere. Existing single-exposure HDR-NVS methods either (1) learn flexible MLP-based CRFs MonoHDR that fit the observed exposure yet neither generalize well to unseen ones nor ensure the expected monotonicity (i.e. LDR intensity grows with input irradiance) EMoR ; or (2) fix a heuristically selected CRF per scene SeHDR that risks response mismatch and precludes training-time adaptation. Single-exposure HDR-NVS thus needs a learnable CRF prior that regularizes response beyond the supervised range, guarantees monotonicity, and promotes plausible responses while retaining scene adaptability. r 0.45 fig:view_inconsist In response, we propose PriorGS, a novel single-exposure HDR-NVS method based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) GaussianSplats that incorporates LDR-to-HDR reconstruction and CRF priors within a base–gain HDR representation. To incorporate learned LDR-to-HDR reconstruction priors, we supervise HDR rendering at training views using pseudo-HDR targets generated by 2D single-exposure HDR reconstruction methods. However, as these targets are estimated separately per views, they may exhibit cross-view inconsistencies. As shown in Figures fig:view_inconsist and fig:apx_abl_direct_hdr , when HDR radiance is encoded directly as Gaussian's color attribute (direct HDR encoding), such inconsistencies impair scene reconstruction, causing severe color and geometry artifacts. To mitigate this, we represent HDR radiance as an LDR base supervised by LDR views and extended to HDR through a 3D gain field. This base-gain representation (1) anchors the scene to the more reliable LDR views while modeling the less reliable HDR extension by the 3D gain field, thereby promoting robustness to cross-view inconsistencies (Figures fig:view_inconsist and fig:apx_abl_direct_hdr ); and (2) enables post-training HDR appearance editing in 3D without altering the LDR base. Next, we regularize CRF modeling with a learnable prior derived from a database of CRFs EMoR . The CRF then re-exposes HDR renderings to match the same LDR views, closing an LDR-base HDR re-exposed LDR loop that anchors HDR recovery to accurate LDR reconstruction at both ends. Our contributions can be summarized as: (1) We propose PriorGS, a novel 3DGS-based single-exposure HDR-NVS framework that guides HDR reconstruction with learned LDR-to-HDR reconstruction priors while enforcing consistent LDR reconstruction before and after HDR recovery; (2) We introduce a base-gain 3D HDR representation that factors scene radiance into an LDR base and an overlaid 3D gain field, promoting robustness to cross-view pseudo-HDR inconsistencies and enabling HDR appearance editing in 3D; (3) We regularize CRF modeling in single-exposure HDR-NVS with a learnable prior, guaranteeing monotonicity and promoting plausible responses while retaining scene adaptability; and (4) Extensive experiments demonstrate that PriorGS substantially outperforms existing methods both quantitatively and qualitatively. Related Works HDR Novel View Synthesis seeks to reconstruct HDR scenes from either (1) LDR captures HDR_Nerf, ltm-nerf, HDRGS, NeXF ; (2) RAW images rawnerf, rawgs, 3dgs-in-the-dark, hdrsplat ; or (3) event–image pairs event1, event2 . We target the first as LDR images are easier to acquire and more widely available. Most LDR-based methods require multi-exposure LDR captures to jointly learn HDR radiance and LDR re-exposure HDRGS , with recent approaches exploring unified 3D and 2D local tone-mapping GaussHDR , physically-inspired appearance modeling PhysHDR , and color-geometry-exposure disentanglement expo-gs . However, these methods rely on multi-exposure supervision and thus do not address the underconstrained nature of single-exposure HDR-NVS. This limitation, together with tedious acquisition of multi-exposure images has motivated recent HDR-NVS methods using more accessible single-exposure LDR inputs SeHDR, MonoHDR . Among single-exposure methods, SeHDR SeHDR fuses bracketed 3D Gaussians into an HDR representation, whereas Mono-HDR-GS MonoHDR learns MLP-based LDR-to-HDR and HDR-to-LDR mappings. However, without HDR GT, their HDR radiance recovery remains underconstrained, lacking direct guidance for accurate HDR reconstruction and thus leading to unreliable recovery. Outside exposure-controllable HDR-NVS, PanoHDR-NeRF PanoHDR-NeRF and GaSLight GasLight use LDR-to-HDR predictions to train 3D HDR representations for relighting. In contrast, PriorGS anchors prior-guided HDR recovery to accurate LDR reconstruction and re-exposure through closed-loop reconstruction. Finally, HDR-NVS requires reliable CRF modeling for re-exposure at unseen exposures. title: Dreams Are Cheaper Than Flights: Curated World-Model Data Improves Aerial Detection
summary: Robot perception is increasingly data driven, yet field data is slow, costly, and sometimes disruptive to collect. Video world models offer a cheaper source: seeded with real frames, they extend a recorded scene into new footage with the deployment's sensor, altitude, and environment. We ask whether such synthetic data matches the utility of real field data and whether detectors trained with it perform in the field. Seeding a 7B-parameter world model with wildlife drone video, we more than double the training set with curated frames. On held-out videos from the same drones, mAP@50--95 rises 4.3\% when these frames are added to real data and 10.3\% when they replace it, and up to 33.5\% on an urban benchmark. Although an expert rejects an estimated 87.5\% of generated clips, the data costs about \$1,100 of GPU time, against more than \$3,200 of field labor alone for a less useful real training set. Synthetic data thus shifts data costs from fieldwork to compute.
