Synthetic data thus shifts data costs from fieldwork to compute. Introduction sec:intro Modern robot perception is trained rather than engineered, and its reliability tracks the quantity and diversity of the data behind it. For field robots this dependence is expensive. Autonomous drones that detect and follow animal herds for ecological monitoring~ kline2026wildwing,kline2025edge,kline2025collective need low-altitude video of the species, sites, and behaviors they will encounter, collected within permits, weather windows, and flight-safety rules~ maalouf2026sora and without disturbing the animals under study~ afridi2025disturbance . The MMLA dataset required more than 150 person-hours of fieldwork on two continents to record 37 videos~ kline_mmla_2025 , and comparable campaigns underlie other wildlife drone datasets~ kholiavchenko2024kabr,kline2025smartwilds . Even so, such datasets cover few herds, days, and poses, and models trained in such small-data regimes generalize poorly~ stevens2025datagap . Simulation is robotics' long-standing answer to scarce data. Rendered simulators make data cheap but must cross a reality gap, typically by randomizing appearance until the real world looks like one more variation~ tobin2017domain . This presumes a simulator that can render the target, which is hard for animals in unstructured terrain. Generative models offer a different trade. Diffusion-generated images improve recognition with scarce real data~ he2023synthetic,trabucco2023effective and augment robot learning data~ chen2023genaug,yu2023rosie , flow-based interpolation densifies sparse aerial imagery~ katole2025orthofuse , and video world models roll a scene forward from a few real frames~ ha2018world,yang2024unisim,bruce_genie_2024,nvidia_cosmos_2025 . Seeded with field footage, such a model yields clips that inherit the sensor, altitude, and environment of the source, which we call field-seeded data. Generated data is not free of risk: world models still produce visible deformities, such as duplicated heads (Fig.~ fig:failures ), and models trained on generated data can lose the tails of the real distribution~ shumailov2024collapse . Synthetic clips must therefore be curated, and because curation follows generation, every rejected clip has already consumed its full compute budget. This raises a practical question rarely answered with numbers: despite high rejection rates, is synthetic data still cheaper than returning to the field? This paper asks whether synthetic data generated from field seeds can provide the fidelity and accuracy of real field data, and whether detectors trained with it perform well on real field footage. We answer both with a field-to-simulation-to-field protocol in which a world model is seeded only from training videos, an expert curates its output, and detectors are tested on held-out videos from the same drones, so that the training data is the only variable. We also price it against fieldwork. Methodology sec:method Our protocol begins and ends in the field (Fig.~ fig:pipeline ). We seed a world model with training footage, curate its output, and test detectors trained with and without it on held-out video from the same drones. We generate with ~ nvidia_cosmos_2025 , an open world foundation model that continues a video from conditioning frames. Each generation is seeded with nine consecutive training frames and a short text prompt describing the scene, and produces a clip of about 120 frames under the model's default sampler settings. Because the seed fixes the camera, altitude, terrain, and illumination, the model invents how the scene evolves, not what it looks like, which avoids most of the appearance gap that rendered simulators close by randomization~ tobin2017domain . Generated clips fail in ways that a domain expert recognizes at once but a detector would absorb as features: distorted or duplicated anatomy, bodies or vehicles that merge or vanish, and motion that violates physics (Fig.~ fig:failures ). A human expert therefore reviews every clip, rejects any clip with a deformity, and annotates the frames of accepted clips with bounding boxes. Only accepted frames enter training. Curation turns generation into rejection sampling. If a clip costs GPU-seconds to generate and is accepted with probability , the expected compute per accepted clip and the fraction of compute spent on rejected clips are The first quantity scales with , which diffusion acceleration reduces. The second is set by the world model's failure rate in the target domain, which acceleration leaves untouched. We apply this protocol to two drone datasets. MMLA~ kline_mmla_2025 contains 155,074 annotated frames from 37 low-altitude videos recorded at Ol Pejeta and Mpala in Kenya and The Wilds in Ohio with DJI Air~2S, DJI Mini, and Parrot Anafi drones. Following the benchmark protocol, we split it into training and test partitions and subsample the training partition to 20,618 frames with 85,967 boxes of zebra, giraffe, and onager. The test partition is never used for seeding, prompting, or curation. To test generality beyond wildlife, we repeat the protocol on VisDrone~ zhu2021visdrone : 24,201 training frames of urban drone footage, tested on its official validation split (2,846 frames, 114,132 boxes, ten classes). On MMLA, the expert reviewed every generated clip, and accepted clips yielded 26,702 synthetic frames with 93,004 boxes. The combined training set thus has 2.3 the frames and 2.1 the boxes of the real one. In an expert-labeled 40-clip pilot, five clips passed ( ). On VisDrone, the expert reviewed 300 clips in 45 minutes and accepted 76 ( , 9,204 frames). The 224 rejected clips (27,896 frames) were annotated the same way and serve as an uncurated control. On MMLA we fine-tune YOLO11m~ jocher2024yolo11 for 50 epochs at batch size 96 with the benchmark's hyperparameters. On VisDrone we train YOLOv8m~ jocher2023yolov8 for 80 epochs at batch size 64. Within each dataset the detector, hyperparameters, and test split are fixed, so the training data is the only variable. We report mAP@50--95 on the field test split. Generation ran on one NVIDIA H100 (80\,GB HBM3, 116\,GB system memory) at about 330\,s per clip, priced at \ 1,131). Of this, 143 hours (\ 5.08 rather than \ 191 still pays for rejected clips. Detection on Held-Out Field Video Table~ tab:mmla reports the MMLA training study. mAP@50--95 rises with every increase in synthetic volume, from 0.845 with real data alone to 0.881 (+4.3 ). That is about per 1,000 synthetic frames, or per \ 5,500 at the 2025 median wage of U.S. wildlife biologists (\ 3,210). The synthetic pool, which alone trained a more accurate field detector, cost \ 164 of expert review (about 1,780 clips at 9\,s each, the same rate as on VisDrone). We exclude annotation, which both routes need. Even pricing fieldwork at labor alone, synthetic data is 2.5 times cheaper. It would be about 20 times cheaper without failed generations, since retained clips used only \ 1,100 of GPU time. That is less than the field labor behind a less useful real training set. Two conditions qualify the result. Synthetic output must be curated, and its transfer verified per class, since a poorly rendered class can vanish unnoticed in aggregate accuracy. Future Work sec:future The dominant cost of field-seeded data is waste. An estimated 87.5 of MMLA generation compute (\ 1,131) produced clips that no detector saw. Faster solvers~ song_denoising_2021,lu_dpm-solver++_2023 , distillation~ salimans_progressive_2022 , and within-network early exits~ moon_simple_2024,tang_adadiff_2024 shrink in Eq.~ for every generation alike but leave unchanged. Recovering this compute calls for quality-aware generation that stops failing generations early, with automated checks to relieve the expert. Building such a system is our ongoing work.

title: TRACE: Target-State Risk-Aligned Conditional Execution for Embodied Tracking
summary: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to follow a language-specified person under occlusion, look-alike distractors, and ambiguous instructions. We show that improving tracking persistence can simultaneously increase safety violations. Using a compact 0.6B vision-language-action (VLA) tracker with a frozen backbone, we update only the planner head with proximal policy optimization (PPO). PPO improves success and following rates across all three EVT-Bench settings, but increases the collision rate on distracted tracking because episodes that previously ended in target loss can instead end in contact. We introduce TRACE, an execution-time target-state risk gate that preserves the learned policy and intervenes selectively. A lightweight risk head processes 84 cues, including candidate boxes, identity margins, a learned range-and-bearing probe, and the policy's commands. When the calibrated risk exceeds a threshold, TRACE rescales the translational component of the next waypoint while leaving yaw unchanged. The executed action is identical to PPO's on more than 98% of steps. In paired evaluations on identical episodes, TRACE reduces the distracted-tracking collision rate by 3.96 percentage points, while further improving success and following rates. Matched slowdown controls without target-state timing do not reproduce this improvement. Concurrent evaluation reproduces a collision reduction of 3.77 points, compared with 0.29 points for identical-arm null pairs, indicating that the effect exceeds evaluation variability. These results show that target-state-aware execution can recover the safety cost of policy post-training with minimal intervention.

Introduction sec:intro Embodied visual tracking (EVT) requires an agent to continuously follow a language-specified person from egocentric observations over long horizons~ luo2018sarl,zhong2024evt,zhang2025trackvla . The task requires the joint solution of target identification, temporal association, and motion planning under occlusion, look-alike distractors, and ambiguous instructions. Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and robot control~ brohan2022rt1,brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0 . The strongest reported results on EVT-Bench come from a B-scale model trained on large-scale data~ zhang2025trackvla , whereas deployment favors compact models with limited adaptation cost and low execution overhead. We construct a compact three-stage tracking system based on a frozen Qwen3-0.6B backbone. The supervised base model keeps the vision encoder, language backbone, and recognition adapter fixed, while a planner head predicts eight future waypoints. We then apply PPO~ schulman2017ppo,schulman2015gae only to the planner head, which improves success and following rates across all three EVT-Bench settings: the planner head is an effective control point for tracking persistence, and the representation backbone need not be updated. The improvement carries a safety cost in distracted tracking. Relative to the supervised model, PPO reduces early target loss but increases collisions, changing the terminal outcome of some episodes from target loss to physical contact (Figure~ fig:teaser A). This observation exposes a limitation of optimizing persistence with a scalar task reward. Existing safe-control and recovery methods~ achiam2017cpo,ray2019safetygym,johannink2019residual,thananjeyan2021recoveryrl,ames2019cbf,dalal2018safe typically impose geometric constraints or respond to local collision conditions. They do not explicitly model the target-state uncertainty that precedes collisions during distracted tracking. In our experiments, a distance-only execution filter does not recover the safety degradation introduced by PPO ( sec:why_not_reward ). These results motivate an execution-time mechanism that uses the tracker's target-state estimate to intervene selectively while preserving the persistence learned by PPO. We therefore introduce , a target-state risk gate applied after policy prediction (Figure~ fig:teaser B). A lightweight head receives target-related cues, including candidate bounding boxes, identity margins, a learned range-and-bearing probe, and the policy's commands and predicted waypoints. The head produces a collision-risk score. Once the score exceeds a calibrated threshold, rescales the translational component of the next waypoint while preserving its yaw component. At all other steps, the executed action is identical to the PPO action. The gate reduces the distracted-tracking collision rate (CR) from to , below the supervised baseline, while further improving success and following rates (SR, FR). Related Work sec:related Embodied visual tracking. Early work casts the task as reinforcement learning over egocentric observations~ luo2018sarl,luo2019rl , later hardened against evasive targets and occlusion by adversarial and structured variants~ zhong2019advat,zhong2021ts,zhong2023rspt . A second line decouples the problem into a visual tracker and a controller, pairing detection or re-identification with image-based servoing~ gupta2016ibvs,bhat2019dimp,maalouf2024followanything . TrackVLA~ zhang2025trackvla instead unifies recognition and planning in a single B model and releases EVT-Bench, and TrackVLA++~ liu2025trackvlapp extends it with explicit reasoning and memory. Both train large backbones end-to-end for the task. In contrast, we hold a compact frozen-backbone tracker fixed and ask what post-training its planner head alone does to collision behavior. Appendix~ app:related covers the adjacent literature on robot following, social navigation, and pursuit--evasion. Post-training and runtime safety. Post-training a supervised policy with on-policy RL is standard practice for language, vision-language, and embodied controllers~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0 , with PPO and generalized advantage estimation the usual choice~ schulman2017ppo,schulman2015gae . Safety is typically added as a separate channel that edits or constrains a proposed action: control-barrier functions~ ames2019cbf , learned safety layers~ dalal2018safe , recovery policies~ thananjeyan2021recoveryrl , residual corrections~ johannink2019residual , and constrained MDPs that fold the constraint into the objective~ achiam2017cpo,ray2019safetygym . Each of these reads geometry, known dynamics, or a constraint signal defined independently of the followed person. In contrast, we condition the intervention on the tracker's own estimate of the target's state, which is the quantity that changes when persistent following turns into contact. Pretrained components and simulation benchmarks. The quantities our risk head reads are produced by components we do not retrain: re-identification confidence from tracking-by-detection pipelines~ wojke2017deepsort,zhang2022bytetrack , frozen vision-language backbones~ radford2021clip,oquab2023dinov2,bai2025qwen25vl , and waypoint heads of the kind used in diffusion and transformer policies~ ho2020ddpm,chi2023diffusionpolicy,zhao2023act . At each step , the agent receives a language instruction that specifies the target and an egocentric RGB history . A compact VLA tracker maps to an waypoint sequence , where each waypoint is . Only the first waypoint is executed through a PD controller, after which the agent observes again and replans. An episode is successful when the agent keeps the described target within the evaluator's following band without terminating in collision. Our goal is to increase persistence without converting lost-target failures into collisions. The construction has three components: a compact supervised tracker whose recognition components are then frozen ( sec:tracker ), PPO on its planner head alone ( sec:ppo ), and a gate that rescales the next waypoint only when the risk score is high ( sec:risk_shield ; Figure~ fig:main_overview ). Each component leaves the previous one unchanged, so we can measure the effect of each separately. The limitation is persistence rather than recognition: most failures are episodes in which the target is dropped early and never recovered, rather than episodes in which the wrong person is followed. title: Cross-Embodiment Motion Planning by Coupling Body-Agnostic World Model with Differentiable Ego-Dynamics
summary: Motion planning in clutter is embodiment-specific: the feasible free space and reachable commands depend on each robot's geometry and dynamics. Existing cross-embodiment policies output normalized commands that disregard these differences, or compensate through per-robot training and distillation. World models can in principle pool cross-embodiment data, yet command-conditioned models bind their latent dynamics to a single action space, while pose-conditioned models omit the mapping from commands to body-specific motion. On flat ground, however, embodiment affects the planner's observations only through the camera ego-motion. Introduction sec:intro obile robots vary widely in embodiment, from wheeled bases and quadrupeds to humanoids and wheeled-legged platforms, yet they share the core problem of local motion planning: generating velocity commands that steer the robot toward a nearby goal through cluttered environments without collision. Global planning produces a route that is largely embodiment-agnostic, whereas local planning must respect each robot's geometry and dynamics: the geometry constrains which gaps are passable, and the dynamics govern which commands can be executed in time. A cross-embodiment local planner must therefore account for these body-specific properties without requiring a dedicated training stage or dataset for each robot. Shared-interface policies output normalized commands and delegate execution to each robot's low-level controller~ 10610665,11696748,ICLR2026_ceb45c48 , leaving the planner blind to the robot's dynamics. Embodiment-aware policies restore dynamics awareness through per-robot training, whether by distilling specialists~ 11244111,11696012 or by attaching residual modules trained with reinforcement learning~ 11696012,ICLR2026_514bdfb1 , so each new robot needs its own training stage. LLM agents , decentralized planning, multi-agent task allocation, cyber-physical systems Introduction Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as the decision-makers of multi-agent teams, from software agents that solve tasks together~ guo2024large,shen2023hugginggpt,zhan2026agensh,hong2024metagpt to robot teams that divide work and plan joint actions~ kannan2024smart,mandi2024roco . In robotics, this division of work is studied as multi-robot task allocation, the question of which robot should execute which task~ gerkey2004formal . Many LLM teams allocate tasks through a central component, such as an orchestrator that delegates work or a single LLM that assigns subtasks to the whole robot team~ yang2025agentnet,kannan2024smart . Central coordination brings scalability bottlenecks and a single point of failure, which leaves the team exposed when the coordinator fails or becomes overloaded~ yang2025agentnet . Decentralized multi-agent LLM systems remove this component. Each agent decides from its own local information and communicates directly with its peers~ tran2025survey . Without an orchestrator, the agents of AgentNet~ yang2025agentnet reached higher accuracy than centralized multi-agent baselines on mathematics, logical question-answering and function-calling benchmarks, and robot arms with one LLM agent each proposed sub-task plans and paths through dialogue~ mandi2024roco . The evidence is not one-sided. In multi-robot planning tasks, Chen et al.~ chen2024scalable compared four designs for coordinating the LLMs of a robot team. The robots in the study cooperated without opponents, and each LLM agent was assumed to know the full environment. In the decentralized architecture, agents relay messages through a peer-to-peer network and achieve consensus via sequential debate rounds—iterative challenge-response exchanges designed to verify reasoning steps and organically converge on consistent information. This setup had the lowest success rate, below a central planner, while hybrid designs did best and the central planner scaled worst as robots were added. In a separate study, Kim et al.~ kim2025scaling evaluated 260 agent-system configurations and found that independent agents, which do not communicate, amplified errors more than centrally coordinated ones, and whether coordination helped depended on the task. Network degradation and agent attrition are unavoidable in distributed multi-agent systems, so we directly compare centralized and decentralized LLM coordination under these conditions. We study this problem in an adversarial game that serves as a simple abstraction of a cyber-physical system, aiming toward applications where an LLM in a hierarchical control setting decides and allocates tasks as an intruder approaches. In perimeter defense, a team of defenders must intercept intruders before they reach a protected region~ shishika2020review , and the intruders score for each one that gets through~ shishika2020cooperative . We call an intruder's entry into the protected region a breach. Perimeter defense belongs to the broader family of pursuit-evasion and reach-avoid differential games~ jaleel2020distributed , in which a team of intruders attempts to reach a target region while defenders attempt to capture or neutralize them~ chung2011search,weintraub2023range,weintraub2020introduction,zhou2025control . Game-theoretic analyses build team strategies by decomposing the game into local games between small groups and assigning defenders to intruders~ shishika2020cooperative , and learned policies imitate a maximum-matching assignment from each defender's local perception~ lee2023gnn . In scenarios such as counter-drone defense, defenders must detect intruders with limited sensing~ park2021antidrone , share observations over a communication network~ maity2024target , and cope with message loss over non-ideal channels~ otte2020auctions . Assigning defenders to intruders is therefore an allocation decision made under partial and evolving information, where the contextual reasoning of LLM planners can be beneficial. Acharya et al.~ acharya2026capture propose a hierarchical architecture in which a per-team LLM planner assigns tactical roles to robots under partial observability, with execution delegated to low-level model predictive controllers. Foundation models~ bommasani2021opportunities , including large language models (LLMs) and vision-language-action models, have been applied across many aspects of robotics, from semantic perception to end-to-end control~ firoozi2025foundation,hu2023toward . A common pattern is hierarchical: a language model plans at a high level while lower-level skills or controllers execute the plan~ ahn2022can,julg2025refined . One reason is speed as inference latency is a recognized obstacle to deploying foundation models on robots~ firoozi2025foundation . Our study follows a hierarchical control design (cf.~ matni2024towards ): in our study a call to the LLM planner took a median of 2.0\,s, while model predictive control (MPC)~ morari2015predictive,mayne2000constrained converts each agent's task into accelerations every 0.1\,s, with a barrier constraint keeping agents collision-free except for when a defender is pursuing to neutralize an intruder. A second design choice is how much of each decision the LLM makes itself rather than leaving it to fixed rules, which we call its authority. At low authority the LLM chooses among options written in advance, as when SayCan~ ahn2022can selects a robot's next skill from a fixed set, which makes each step of the plan interpretable. At high authority it sets numbers that a solver then uses, as when an LLM writes the weights of a reward that MPC optimizes~ yu2023language . That design solved more robot tasks than an LLM that composed predefined skills, and its authors note that constraining what the LLM may set makes the system more stable at some cost in flexibility~ yu2023language . Our aim is to study how LLM-driven teams compete against each other in an adversarial game, and how centralized, and decentralized planners, with different levels of authority, compare under different communication conditions. How a team allocates tasks determines what it needs from its communication network. A central allocator can in principle find the best assignment by gathering all information and planning for the whole team, but it has high communication demands and is a single point of failure~ dias2006market . When radio range is limited, reports and orders must be relayed, and a partitioned network cuts agents off from both. Fully distributed allocation avoids this round trip, but good local choices may not add up to a good team assignment~ dias2006market , and agents that each pick their best task can pick the same one~ gerkey2004formal . Market-based methods combine the two by letting agents bid for tasks~ dias2006market . The consensus-based auction algorithm (CBAA) reaches a conflict-free assignment through local message exchange alone and tolerates inconsistent information across the team~ choi2009consensus . Auction methods with conventional bids have been tested under lossy and fading communication~ otte2020auctions,lott2026decentralized , and LLM teams have been compared under centralized, decentralized and hybrid communication on cooperative planning tasks~ chen2024scalable . By framing the problem as an adversarial game, we let teams of LLMs compete directly against one another, and we compare a central LLM commander with decentralized LLM agents that resolve allocation conflicts through a consensus auction, under progressively degraded communication networks. We also evaluate both architectures when some agents submit falsified estimates (Section~ sec:methods:comms ). In a typical airspace, defender agents share the sky with birds and civilian drones, and detecting drones, birds, and other distractors is the subject of a dedicated benchmark challenge~ coluccia2021drone . A textual state-based only defender treats birds, civilian drones and intruders the same way, i.e. as contacts. We refer to birds and civilian drones as non-hostile contacts. Without a recognition and classification mechanism, the defender cannot tell the intruders apart from the non-hostile contacts. And, pursuing a non-hostile contact costs more than just time as a defender that touches any contact is lost, resulting in reduction of defensive capacity. Multimodal LLMs, which accept images in addition to text, can inspect a contact before deciding whether to engage it, but whether this ability helps the team depends on two factors: the model must correctly classify the object, and the coordination interface must allow it to act on that judgment. Using image-based contact classification, we consider four contact types (birds, civilian drones, intruder drones, and disguised intruder drones) and ask how centralized and decentralized LLM teams, each run with both a low-cost and a near-frontier model, handle these contacts under the communication conditions studied above. We deliberately keep the perception component simple: the aim is a reproducible benchmark for multimodal LLM decision-making in adversarial games, in which the effects of team architecture and communication degradation can be isolated from perception difficulty. Here we compare three LLM-coordinated defender teams that differ in where LLM decision-making is placed within the defensive architecture (Fig.~ fig:architecture ). The first, the commander team, places all authority in a central commander, whose LLM assigns tasks to every agent. The second, the consensus team, has decentralized agents that bid for tasks and agree on who takes which through a consensus-based auction. Each agent’s LLM adjusts its own bids according to its authority. At low authority it can only choose a weight profile, a priority for each intruder and up to three preferred tasks. At high authority it sets the weights of the bid formula and a multiplier from 0 to 2 for each intruder’s pursuit value. title: Contact-based optimization for collision-free motion planning for a million robots
summary: Multi-agent robotic systems have attracted growing interest in recent years, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows to autonomous operations on land, in the air, and on water. At the planning level, robot motion is often modeled using double-integrator dynamics (with low-level controllers handling the physical dynamics during execution) with a minimum-energy objective subject to collision-avoidance constraints and limits on position, velocity, and acceleration. The complexity of the problem resides in the constraints, which couple the trajectories and make the optimization problem nonconvex. Existing numerical approaches typically discretize and optimize entire trajectories, which becomes expensive for large fleets. We exploit the structure of optimal trajectories by organizing optimization around contacts, at which robots reach the minimum allowed separation. We formulate a coupled algebraic system in contact variables and reconstruct trajectories analytically between contacts. Our algorithm, sequential contact insertion (SCI), starts from unconstrained trajectories, inserts contacts at separation violations, and jointly adjusts their times and states. Numerical experiments demonstrate planning for one million robots in minutes and thousands of robots in fractions of a second. On problems feasible for a fixed-grid sequential convex programming baseline, SCI achieves median speedups of several orders of magnitude at matching solution accuracy.

title: A complete analytical characterization of optimal collision-free motion for two robots
summary: Collision-free motion planning for multi-agent robotic systems remains an active research area because of the complexity of coordinating robot trajectories, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows to autonomous operations on land, in the air, and on water. Importantly, the analytical difficulty of nonconvex collision-avoidance constraints has so far driven the development of exclusively numerical methods. We derive a complete analytical characterization of the optimal trajectories for two robots that start and end at rest, under double-integrator dynamics and a squared-acceleration objective. We prove that these trajectories belong to eight distinct contact families and determine which family applies for each configuration of initial and final positions. We analyze the geometrical properties of the optimal trajectories, provide a numerical algorithm for computing them, and discuss how these insights may improve the performance of existing numerical trajectory optimizers.

title: VLA Policies Do Not Know When Not to Act: Unintended Task Execution and Start Suppression
summary: A robot should act only on an instruction from a person or on an intent that the robot explicitly represents and generates. Unintended actions taken without such an instruction can cause risk or inconvenience to people and the environment. We examine how recent vision-language-action (VLA) policies respond when the instruction is missing or meaningless. We apply a paired protocol with empty, neutral, nonsense, infeasible, and wrong-task instructions to six model checkpoints in LIBERO-Goal simulation. Holding the initial state fixed and varying only the instruction, we ask three questions: whether the robot starts to move, which task it completes, and what the instruction determines. Even when the instruction was empty, the robot started moving in every episode with all six checkpoints, and with five of them it often completed a task that the instruction had not specified. On two GR00T checkpoints, the instruction determined which task was executed but not whether the robot started moving; the robot moved even on infeasible instructions. We then tested three methods for suppressing the start: prepending "if no task is given do not move" to the instruction; a gate that holds the robot when the first action chunk for the given instruction nearly equals that for an empty instruction; and fine-tuning the policy to hold still on non-task inputs. The prefix stopped the robot in none of the six checkpoints, and the gate held it on non-task inputs in five of the six checkpoints. The fine-tuned policy never completed a task on non-task inputs, but it did not reliably keep the robot still, and it failed to suppress the start on infeasible instructions.

The fine-tuned policy never completed a task on non-task inputs, but it did not reliably keep the robot still, and it failed to suppress the start on infeasible instructions. Introduction sec:intro We expect a robot to begin a task only after a person has given it an explicit instruction. A robot that starts without such an instruction may perform actions that its user did not intend, such as handing over an object before the person is ready~ xu2026assist or picking up an object after an observed event that calls for no action~ liu2026proactive . Acting without an instruction is appropriate only when the context explicitly permits it, and that context should not be left implicit in the policy's weights. The robot should explicitly represent and generate the intent on which it acts, namely what it is about to do and whether to start now, and the action should follow from that representation rather than from the arrival of an input. Proactive Robot Assistance~ liu2026proactive is an example in which the judgment is generated explicitly, by a vision-language model reasoning over a state change, before any instruction-free action. The vision-language-action (VLA) policies studied here have no such representation. They map camera images, proprioception, and a language instruction to robot actions, and the recipe that trains them does not address the requirement. Language-conditioned behavior cloning pairs every training input with a demonstrated action~ brohan2022rt1,jang2022bcz . Each demonstration begins with a task instruction and ends when that task is completed, and some data pipelines also remove the stationary (``no-op'') steps in which the robot does not move~ kim2024openvla . As a result, the training data contain no sample in which the policy is asked to hold. A policy trained this way emits an action chunk for every input, including the inputs that a deployed robot meets when the instruction channel is empty, corrupted, or names something on which the robot cannot act. Examples are a speech-recognition result that was dropped, an unrelated sentence picked up from a nearby conversation, and a request that refers to an object that is not present. What the policy does in these states is specified neither by the recipe nor by the standard evaluation, which measures whether the robot does what it is asked to do by reporting the fraction of episodes in which the instructed task is completed. This evaluation does not measure whether the robot performs tasks that it was not asked to perform. When the designated task is not completed, the policy may have held still, may have attempted the designated task and failed, or may have completed a different task. A robot that, given no executable instruction, selects and completes one of the tasks available in the scene performs an unintended action; a robot that holds still does not. The two outcomes carry different consequences for the people and objects around the robot. Several studies have removed or corrupted the instruction and reported either a drop in success or little change in behavior. grant2026notall report LIBERO-Goal designated-task success of 12.0 or lower under an empty string for OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025oft , X-VLA~ zheng2025xvla , and ~ pi2025pi05 . LIBERO-PRO~ zhou2025liberopro reports that policy outputs remain nearly unchanged under corrupted instructions, and LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025liberoplus reports that language perturbations cause the second-smallest average drop in success among its seven perturbation types. In a scene where several tasks are feasible, both results are consistent with a third outcome: the policy completes a default task that the instruction never specified. Two studies have observed this outcome. In LIBERO-CF~ fang2026overrides , the grasp positions of under an empty instruction stay centered on the object of the scene's well-learned training task. xie2026language evaluate the goal predicates of every LIBERO-Goal task and report that OpenVLA-OFT and , given gibberish or an empty string, execute one default task. OpenVLA-OFT, for example, turns on the stove or puts the bowl on the stove. Neither study measured whether the policy starts at all, which is the quantity to which the requirement above refers. The outcome concerns intent alignment, because the task the robot executes is not one it was asked to execute, and, as we show, the presence of a command string is not evidence that it was asked. The outcome is also relevant to safety, because the robot moves and makes contact where a person has reason to expect it to hold. The requirement leads to three measurement questions, each asked on identical initial states: whether the policy starts at all, which task it completes, and what the instruction determines when one is present. Our protocol (Section~ sec:protocol ) checks the goal predicate of every task in the scene, as xie2026language also do, separates a non-start (the arm stays within 5~cm, touches nothing, and completes nothing) from motion without contact and from a failed attempt, and runs every condition on the same initial states and seeds, so comparisons are paired by episode. We applied it to six LIBERO-tuned checkpoints from five model families, five public and one fine-tuned by us (Table~ tab:ckpt ), under empty, neutral, nonsense, infeasible, and wrong-task instructions, and to three start-suppression mechanisms: an instruction prefix, a first-call action-difference gate, and no-action fine-tuning (Section~ sec:mechanisms ). Start suppression means any addition to or around a policy that is meant to keep it from starting when no executable task is specified; we judge it by the non-start rate. This paper makes three contributions. It measures whether a VLA policy starts, separately from which task it completes, and shows that none of six LIBERO-tuned checkpoints from five model families holds still under an empty instruction. Every checkpoint started moving in every episode (non-start 0.0 for each), and five of the six completed one of the scene's tasks in 30.5--94.0 of episodes (Section~ sec:failure ). It shows that the instruction selects the task but does not control the start. As a result, a safeguard that holds the robot only when the instruction is empty does not stop it when the instruction cannot be executed. On the two GR00T checkpoints, sentences that describe impossible actions still led to an unintended completion in 61.0--73.0 of episodes (Sections~ sec:language and~ sec:interlock ). It compares three start-suppression mechanisms under one protocol, and reports the inputs on which each mechanism fails. No-action fine-tuning prevented contact in all three training seeds but kept the arm in place reliably in only one (Sections~ sec:results , sec:effect , and~ sec:bound ). The evaluation code, the episode records of every experiment, the analysis scripts, and an evaluation kit that implements the protocol are released at . Related Work sec:related sec:rw-decline Prior work that degrades or removes the instruction reports designated-task success. grant2026notall report success under a null prompt for five VLAs, LIBERO-PRO~ zhou2025liberopro finds policy outputs nearly unchanged under corrupted instructions, LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025liberoplus finds that language perturbations reduce success less than most other perturbations, LangGap~ hou2026langgap observes that most LIBERO suites assign one task per layout, and LIBERO-CF~ fang2026overrides and ICBench~ zhang2026restoring report that, under a counterfactual or contradictory instruction, policies often complete the scene's well-learned training task (LIBERO-CF) or a visually plausible task (ICBench). emukpere2026robust argue that success should be split into execution and target selection, and zhan2026stable report 11.4 blank-instruction success for on LIBERO-Goal. Two studies are closest to ours. xie2026language hold the initial state fixed, swap in the instruction of another task in the same scene, degrade it to gibberish and an empty string, and judge which task was completed by evaluating every task's goal predicates. On LIBERO-Goal, OpenVLA-OFT completes the swapped task in 97 of episodes, and under gibberish or an empty string OpenVLA-OFT and execute one default task. jiang2026encoded replace the target object named in LIBERO-Object instructions and find that , GR00T~N1.7, , and LingBot-VA direct 86.5--98.3 of trials to the original target. These studies establish two observations: LIBERO-tuned policies execute a default task under an empty or meaningless instruction~ fang2026overrides,xie2026language , and on LIBERO-Goal they follow the instruction of another task in the same scene~ xie2026language . None of these works reports how often the policy does not start, and none evaluates a mechanism for preventing the start. Our protocol adds both. Our gate uses the contrast between the instruction-conditioned and the instruction-free prediction that LIBERO-CF and zhan2026stable use to strengthen language conditioning, but it thresholds the contrast once per episode to decide whether to start. A second line of work treats declining to act as a safety behavior~ hou2026conflictvla,yeke2026yesman,song2025rationalvla,hsieh2025dowhat,izzo2026actthink,singh2026bokbo . These works ask whether a policy refuses an invalid instruction or an unsafe action; we ask the prior question of whether the policy avoids starting when no executable instruction is given. Our prefix, gate, and fine-tuning are counterparts of the defensive prompt of yeke2026yesman , the execution-withholding layer of singh2026bokbo , and the rejection path of song2025rationalvla . title: When the Simulator Fails, Not the Policy: Auditing Contact Artifacts in Simulated Robot Benchmarks
summary: Simulation benchmarks score robot policies by success rate, and every failed episode counts against the policy. Many of these failures are the simulator's fault, not the policy's; we find the cause and fix it. Testing a vision language action model and a world action model in simulation, we find that the policy often places the object and the simulator then ejects it, and that the benchmark's own scripted demonstrations fail the same way. We present SimuGuard, an auditing plugin for LIBERO, RoboTwin, RoboCasa and RoboDojo. It leaves the evaluation unchanged. At every physics step, it records the state and flags an object that starts moving at a contact faster than the robot's contact or gravity account for. It replays a recorded episode bit for bit, and it reruns the episode with one simulation parameter changed. With it we trace these episodes on RoboTwin to the collision detection of the physics engine: for geometry one to two centimeters apart, the engine reports a penetration of about two centimeters, and the solver throws the object out at several meters per second. The cause is one constant: the distance algorithm discards triangles below a fixed area threshold, which valid triangles fall below at the centimeter scale. With that constant changed and nothing else, episodes with an artifact fall from 12 in 100 to none, and the success rate on five container tasks rises from 89% to 98%. Success rates in simulation thus count failures that the simulator causes. Benchmarks on PhysX 5.3.1 or earlier should rerun in a repaired engine. Where the engine cannot change, they should report the success rate together with the range it spans when every flagged episode fails or passes: 75.8% to 98.5% around a reported 83.1% for LingBot-VA.

Introduction sec:intro Simulation benchmarks give a repeatable way to compare robot policies, from vision language action (VLA) models to world action models~ brohan2023rt2,brohan2023rt1,octo2024,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,bjorck2025gr00t,geminirobotics2025,li2026lingbotva . LIBERO~ liu2023libero , RoboCasa~ nasiriany2024robocasa and RoboTwin~ mu2025robotwin,chen2025robotwin2 fix the tasks and the protocol and treat the simulator as faithful physics. Their success rates record which episodes failed, not why. A failure caused by the simulator's treatment of contact enters the same count as a failure caused by the policy. Testing a world action model and a VLA in simulation, we find that such failures are frequent: the policy places the object, and the simulator throws it out. In an episode of RoboTwin~2.0's Place Can Basket, LingBot-VA~ li2026lingbotva places a can inside the basket, resting against its wall. The gripper releases it. After 0.28\,s, within a single 4\,ms physics step, PhysX reports a piece of the can 2.75\,cm inside a piece of the basket wall, although the two pieces are 2.1\,cm apart, and the can's speed rises from 0.2 to 22\,m/s while no robot link touches it and the robot is nearly still; the basket ejects it, the can lands 1.65\,m away, and the benchmark records a failure ( ). Nothing in the recording supplies the 2.4\,J the can gains: no robot contact in that step and no drop. Replayed with the same recorded actions and the reported depth removed over several physics steps instead of one, the episode passes the benchmark's own success check ( ); in the engine with one constant of its distance algorithm corrected, the contact is never reported ( ). We call a contact response that sets an object moving faster than the robot's contact or gravity account for a contact artifact. The impulse that starts one lasts a single physics step and falls between two camera frames; a video shows the can flying, not what launched it, and the success check cannot tell whether the policy or the simulator decided the episode. is an auditing plugin that leaves the evaluation unchanged ( ). An adapter attaches it to the benchmark's own evaluation script; we provide adapters for LIBERO, RoboTwin, RoboCasa and RoboDojo. At every physics step it records the actuation, the object states and the contacts, and flags an object that starts moving at a contact faster than the robot's contact or gravity account for. It replays a recorded episode bit for bit by rebuilding the seeded scene and applying the recorded actuation from the first step. A rerun is a replay with one simulation parameter changed, with the recorded actuation and the success check fixed. Prior work adds metrics to the success rate~ wang2025roboeval,snyder2026binary,jiang2026benchmarking or measures how solvers depart from physics~ erez2015simulation,lelidec2023contact ; neither connects an anomalous contact in a rollout to the outcome of that rollout. In short, many failures in simulated robot benchmarks are the simulator's fault, not the policy's; we find the cause and fix it. Our contributions are: A finding and its cause. Simulated benchmarks contain frequent episodes in which the policy has placed the object and the simulator then ejects it, so the benchmark scores a failure of the policy. On five RoboTwin tasks that place objects into containers with thin walls, 40 of LingBot-VA's 44 failures and 6 of HyVLA's 10 contain such an ejection, and the benchmark's own scripted demonstrations, which act on ground truth object poses, fail the same way. title: REA: A Routed Embodied Agent Runtime for Asynchronous Brain-Cerebellum Control
summary: Foundation models are becoming remarkably reliable at high-level reasoning, yet they remain too slow and costly to serve as fine-grained controllers. Conversely, fast policies like VLAs and whole-body controllers offer more efficient reflexes, but struggle to generalize. While pairing a deliberative brain (foundation models) with a reactive cerebellum (fast policies) seems natural for embodied systems, two obstacles remain: methods are built and scored on incompatible stacks, and their asynchronous coordination is difficult. For example, an agent that calls the VLA in the agentic loop can stall the fast execution, while a VLA that calls the agent on errors tends to re-trigger fallbacks repeatedly or completely miss silent failures. To address this, we propose REA (Routed Embodied Agent), a unified runtime where a deliberative System 2, an embodied router System 1 and reactive System 0 policies cooperate under a single golden rule - no running policy waits on the brain. Instead of querying the brain at each failure, REA employs a route memory that stores each policy's measured success ahead of time, a boundary-triggered judge gate that consults the brain on policy execution, and a shared-budget escalation ladder for bounded recovery. Evaluated on 3,000 test episodes across 60 LIBERO-Pro tasks, REA reaches 95.9% success and beats the best single-agent baseline in its own policy pool (94.7%) while reducing control steps by 25% and control time by 17%. In a separate 100-episode RoboTwin 2.0 study, REA achieves 84% success with VLA policies and 86% with VLA+code, compared with 80% for the strongest single VLA baseline MEDex. These results demonstrate learned and programmatic policies operating within the same runtime. REA also transfers to BEHAVIOR-1K and a real Unitree G1 humanoid, achieving the highest observed success among the compared methods.

title: Hierarchical World Models with Implicit Dynamics
summary: Planning with world models enables test-time adaptation for embodied agents, offering superior generalization over direct policy learning. However, long-horizon tasks remain hindered by cumulative errors and search complexity. Existing hierarchical methods often use rigid macro-actions or latent skills, leading to brittle representations and limited fine-grained control. We introduce ID-WM (Implicit Dynamics World Models), a hierarchical world model that decouples state-space reachability from local control. Our framework utilizes a high-level model to sample feasible transitions across the state manifold and a low-level world model as an inverse dynamics solver to ground these transitions into precise actions. This allows the planner to identify reachable subgoals without being constrained by low-level execution details. By prioritizing local physical feasibility over global behavioral patterns, ID-WM synthesizes novel long-horizon plans from short segments, transcending the specific behavioral modes seen during training. We demonstrate its effectiveness across three navigation and manipulation suites, achieving a 38.5% improvement over state-of-the-art policy and diffusion-based planners. Crucially, by leveraging this hierarchical structure to mitigate compounding errors, our approach yields a 135% performance gain over single-level world model MPC, particularly in complex, unseen configurations for long-horizon tasks. Videos can be viewed at https://id-wm.github.io

Introduction World models (WM) ~ truck-backer-upper, wm, lecun2022path have emerged as a powerful paradigm for embodied decision-making~ gaia1, dreamerv4, newt, Li2026CausalWM . By learning predictive models of environment dynamics, they enable test-time reasoning and the synthesis of novel behaviors for unseen goals by searching in the action space~ dinowm, vjepa2, nwm, dexwm . However, planning with WMs faces two fundamental challenges: 1) search complexity grows exponentially with planning horizon, and 2) prediction errors accumulate over long rollouts. Therefore, most WM-based planners are restricted to short-horizon tasks~ dinowm, vjepa2 , rely on simplified action abstractions~ nwm , or operate in high-level spaces such as language, sacrificing fine-grained control~ vlwm . Hierarchical learning offers a principled solution to this scalability challenge by decomposing long-horizon problems into manageable abstractions~ schmidhuber1991learning, Sutton1999BetweenMA, Barto2003RecentAI . It has been extensively studied in Reinforcement Learning (RL)~ FeUdal, hiro, hiql, Pertsch2020AcceleratingRL , where hierarchy mitigates the credit assignment problem in long trajectories, and in imitation learning~ Gupta2019RelayPL,saycan , where it enables reusable behaviors. More recently, hierarchical structure has been introduced into diffusion-based planners to avoid directly modeling entire trajectories~ Li2023HierarchicalDF, hdiffuser, Hao2025CHDCH , improving scalability and generalization beyond fixed-horizon training data. How can we enable the same capabilities for task-agnostic world models, enabling long-horizon zero-shot planning for unseen goals? A direct approach would be to simply increase the prediction horizon or action abstraction (e.g., frame-skipping)~ Zhang2026HierarchicalPW . However, previous attempts at hierarchical world models typically depend on task-specific priors to function effectively, relying on pre-trained skills and low-level policies~ lsp, Pertsch2020AcceleratingRL or rewards and value functions to verify subgoal feasibility~ Gumbsch2024LearningHW, Nasiriany2019PlanningWG . This dependency arises because planning is fundamentally adversarial: without these anchoring constraints, a powerful optimizer will inevitably exploit deficiencies in a learned world model, discovering "wormholes" or unrealistic transitions~ Chua2018DeepRL, psenka2026parallelstochasticgradientbasedplanning . To make hierarchical world models suitable for planning, we must construct a latent space that both condenses trajectory information to minimize search complexity, and remains inherently well-behaved to prevent the planner from exploiting unrealistic transitions. To this end, we introduce , a hierarchical world model with implicit dynamics grounded in the insight that effective planning requires decoupling topological reachability from execution details ( ). consists of a high-level diffusion-based world model that only implicitly models the dynamics by outputting states that are within a fixed distance away from the current state, functioning as a neighboring state generator, and a deterministic low-level model conditioned on both current state and action, acting as an inverse dynamics solver. Conditioned on the current state and a Gaussian noise, the high-level model leverages the generative power of diffusion to map a tractable unit Gaussian latent space to the manifold of feasible neighboring states. This formulation allows us to treat the noise as an implicit high-level action, enabling the planner to search over a well-behaved distribution instead of complex, discontinuous skill spaces to reason purely about "where to go," while the low-level model recovers the precise executable actions for "how to get there." We summarize our contributions as follows: We introduce , a hierarchical world model that decouples reachability from control, eliminating the need for task-specific value functions or pre-trained policies. We propose a corresponding hierarchical planning algorithm that bridges high-level abstraction with local dynamics, enabling robust, long-horizon decision-making. Across three navigation and manipulation environment suites, shows 38.5 improvement for reaching arbitrary goals against powerful hierarchical offline reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and diffusion planning methods, and crucially, a 135 improvement over single-level world model and planning regimes. This paradigm spans policy architectures~ Chung2016HierarchicalMR , reinforcement learning~ FeUdal, hiql, Haramati2026HierarchicalER, Gumbsch2024LearningHW , imitation learning~ Gupta2019RelayPL , and planning~ Nair2019HierarchicalFS, Nasiriany2019PlanningWG . Existing work focuses on both behavioral (skills/options)~ Sutton1999BetweenMA, lsp, Pertsch2020AcceleratingRL, SkiMo, Dalal2021AcceleratingRR, Zhang2023LeveragingJM, puppeteer and subgoal-centric approaches~ HiGoC, Nasiriany2019PlanningWG, hiro . However, these methods typically rely on coupled priors, such as rewards, learned value functions or pre-trained low-level policies~ Nasiriany2019PlanningWG, Haramati2026HierarchicalER ~to ensure feasibility, limiting generalization beyond the training distribution. In contrast, we eliminate this dependency, enabling robust hierarchical reasoning purely through implicit dynamics even when reliable value functions and policies are absent. World Models for Embodied Planning World models~ truck-backer-upper, wm, lecun2022path have emerged as a foundational paradigm for embodied decision-making, enabling agents to reason about the future consequences of their actions. Recently, the field has shifted towards developing general-purpose world models~ genie, dinowm, nwm, sora2, veo3, dreamerv4 capable of capturing broad environmental dynamics, diverging from traditional model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) where learning task-specific reward or value functions is paramount~ dreamer, dreamerv2, dreamerv3, tdmpc, tdmpc2, transformer100k, iris . Once these dynamics are learned, inference-time planning algorithms like the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM)~ cem or gradient descent—are employed to derive behaviors zero-shot~ dinowm, vjepa2, pldm, dexwm . However, the effectiveness of these approaches is often constrained to short horizons due to the computational complexity of search and the accumulation of prediction errors over time. While various strategies have been proposed to mitigate these issues, ranging from robust gradient-based optimization~ robustwmplanning, psenka2026parallelstochasticgradientbasedplanning and efficient sampling routines~ Bharadhwaj2020ModelPredictiveCV to temporal approximations for longer action sequences~ nwm , they remain fundamentally flat in their temporal reasoning. Consequently, they struggle with long-horizon task solving, remaining susceptible to local minima and limited in their scalability to complex behaviors. Concurrently, HWM~ Zhang2026HierarchicalPW builds a hierarchical latent world model by increasing the high-level frameskip and learning macro-actions; in contrast, searches over the diffusion noise space, which is smooth and well-conditioned by construction. title: SACQ: Structure-Aware Codebook Quantization for Ultra-Low-Bit Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable capable robot behavior, but their large memory footprint limits deployment on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Weight quantization is a natural remedy, yet post-training quantization (PTQ) recipes inherited from large language models degrade when applied to VLAs at ultra-low precision. Existing low-bit PTQ methods often fail to explicitly account for the structure of downstream operations and allocate precision without considering its effect on the policy actions. We introduce SACQ, an ultra- low-bit weight-only vector-codebook quantization framework for VLAs. SACQ combines (1) structure-aware codebook fitting with role-specific quadratic metrics that reflect input statistics and downstream sensitivity; (2) action-aware mixed-bit allocation based on the increase in final-action error as individual layers are compressed; and (3) two-stage post-quantization refinement that reassigns codeword indices with second-order error compensation and calibrates codebooks and row-group scales against the decoded action. Using GR00T N1.7, SACQ achieves 93.85% average success across four LIBERO suites at 1.5 bits per language/action weight while reducing model memory by 4.83x. Existing low-bit PTQ methods often fail to explicitly account for the structure of downstream operations and allocate precision without considering its effect on the policy actions. Recent models perform strongly across diverse manipulation tasks, establishing VLAs as an important approach to generalist robot policies. At the same time, VLA models have grown substantially in scale, creating significant memory demands for resource-constrained robotic platforms. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is attractive in this setting because it reduces model memory without requiring full retraining. However, ultra-low-bit VLA quantization is especially challenging because the effect of a weight error depends strongly on where it appears in the policy. For example, errors in query and key projections perturb the attention logits that determine token mixing, whereas errors in feed-forward projections alter the hidden representations passed to subsequent operations. As a result, similar layer-local reconstruction errors can have substantially different consequences depending on where they occur. A related challenge is precision allocation: a layer that appears insensitive under a local reconstruction objective can still have a large effect on the final action. Representative PTQ methods such as GPTQ~ gptq2023 minimize layer-wise reconstruction errors using approximate second-order information. GPTVQ~ gptvq2024 extends this reconstruction-based formulation to vector quantization by incorporating the Hessian of the layer-output reconstruction objective into codeword assignment. Other vector-quantization methods, including AQLM~ aqlm and QuIP ~ quipsharp , further demonstrate the effectiveness of codebook-based representations for extreme LLM compression. However, these methods primarily optimize quantization with respect to layer-local reconstruction and do not explicitly account for the operation in which each projection output is subsequently used. For VLAs, recent quantization methods increasingly incorporate properties of action generation into the quantization process. QVLA~ qvla2026 uses action-related sensitivity to guide mixed-precision allocation, while ActQuant~ actquant2026 combines action-sensitive inter-tensor bit allocation with intra-tensor scale optimization. HBVLA~ hbvla2026 extends VLA weight quantization to the 1-bit regime, while QuantVLA~ quantvla2026 explicitly considers the structure of the diffusion action transformer in its quantization design. title: CausalWAM: Learning the Causes of Actions in World Action Models
summary: World action models (WAMs) learn latent variables from observations and use these to both predict the evolution of the scene and to generate actions. The prediction has to be of the whole scene, whereas only a portion of the scene causes actions. WAMs fitted to demonstrations do not, in general, guarantee that they will generate actions solely from the latent causes of the demonstrated actions (the action-relevant latent variables), as the model could just as well learn to imitate in this way whilst entangling the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance variables. We therefore separate out what causes action from what prediction depends on. We prove that under a sparsity constraint the latent variables used to generate actions are an invertible function of the action-relevant latent variables alone and the true structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables. This requires neither sufficient temporal dependence nor any assumptions on how the unobserved regimes evolve and holds even when the action-relevant latent variables are statistically dependent on the rest. We therefore propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which incorporates the constraint into a pretrained WAM by adding a sparse routing path to its action head, with the world modeling objective remaining unchanged. Experiments on both synthetic data and real-world robots validate the theory as well as showcase the improved efficiency in closed-loop success.

Introduction The action a robot performs when stacking a single block atop another depends on the position of both blocks and the fact that the gripper is currently holding the uppermost block. The camera image's pixels will change significantly if the robot removes the tablecloth or clears away the clutter located behind the table; however, this will have no effect upon the motion itself. WAMs (World Action Models) like Fast-WAM yuan2026fastwam , and Cosmos~3 nvidia2026cosmos3 are able to extract latent variables from images and can be used to generate actions from those latent variables, while also being capable of generating images of potential subsequent frames. Since prediction has to account for the whole scene, these latent variables also describe the tablecloth and the clutter. We refer to the latent variables that cause the demonstrated actions as action-relevant latent variables, and to the others as nuisance variables. =-1 Fitting the demonstrations well does not in itself guarantee that the WAM is acting from the action-relevant latent variables. For each step of the demonstration we could write and where is the latent state, is some unknown invertible function, is some unknown action mechanism and is exogenous noise. Separating action from prediction is then about recovering (up to certain indeterminacies) the action-relevant latent variables and which of those variables cause each action dimension. Without further assumptions, the latent causal variables cannot be identified from their observations hyvarinen1999nonlinear,locatello2019challenging . Observing the actions as well doesn't help with this ambiguity, as two models can give rise to the same distribution of whilst their latent variables differ by an arbitrary invertible transformation. This transformation can mix the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance ones, so a very flexible action head could generate actions from variables which also contain information about the tablecloth (which doesn't in fact cause the motion) and still fit the demonstrations equally well. To make latent variables identifiable, existing works in nonlinear independent component analysis (ICA) introduce auxiliary variables, such as domain or time indices, or exploit temporal dependence hyvarinen2016unsupervised,hyvarinen2017nonlinear,hyvarinen2019nonlinear,khemakhem2020variational . For latent causal processes, identifiability has been established under sufficient temporal dependence yao2022temporally and conditions on the latent dynamics song2023temporally . Interventions with known targets have also been introduced to pin down the latents lippe2022citris . Many of these assumptions might be violated for demonstrations in complex real-world scenarios such as robotics, where some time steps might be independent, the latent dynamics might not be Markov, and controlled interventions are either prohibitively expensive or simply impossible. Another line of research constrains the generative process by restricting the function class or enforcing sparsity in the dependency structure kivva2022identifiability,zheng2022identifiability,lachapelle2022disentanglement . Most of these studies, similar to those previously discussed, aim to recover all latent variables, requiring their conditions to hold even for nuisance variables that a robot can disregard. In contrast, results on partial identifiability focus on a subset of latent variables, determined by side information accompanying the data, such as content shared across views vonkugelgen2021self,yao2024multiview , components invariant across domains kong2022partial , or elements relevant to specific tasks zheng2026generalist . For robots learning from demonstrations, the relevant subset consists of the latent causes underlying the demonstrated actions. Since no view, domain, or task label directly specifies this subset, the actions themselves must indicate which latent variables are pertinent. This raises the following question: From demonstrations alone, can we separate what causes actions from what prediction needs? In this work, we answer this question with a constraint on the action side that leaves prediction free to use every latent variable. Since each action is generated from only part of the latent state, constraining the number of dependencies between latent variables and action dimensions can separate that part from the rest. Specifically, we prove that, without such a constraint and under nondegeneracy conditions, fitting the demonstrations only ensures that each action dimension of the estimated mechanism depends on at least as many latent variables as the true one (Prop. prop:generalist ). We then incorporate a sparsity regularization on the dependency structure between latent state and action variables during estimation. Under the same conditions, the lower bound becomes an equality and the dependency structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables (Thm. thm:action ). Moreover, we prove that the estimated action-relevant variables under the proposed constraint are an invertible function of the ground-truth latent variables causing the true action (Thm. thm:state ). The latent causes of the actions are thus identified as a block and are separated from the nuisance variables. The theoretical guarantee relies purely on observational demonstrations, without requiring any interventions, sufficient temporal dependence, or any assumptions about the latent dynamics. The framework also allows dependence between action-relevant latent variables and the nuisance variables (e.g., a tablecloth could be correlated with the positions of the cubes). According to the established theory, we propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which adds a sparse routing path from the visual and task tokens to the action head in Cosmos~3 and applies a token-level surrogate of the constraint to this path (Sec. sec:method ). In synthetic scenarios, we validate the identifiability claims shown by our theory. On RoboCasa365, LIBERO, and a real Franka R3 robot, the routing path improves aggregate closed-loop success over Cosmos~3 without it, and in most visualized frames its routing mass falls on the object being moved and its target (Sec. sec:experiments ).
